label: Agency & communion (the Big Two)

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Converges across surveys, lab work, cross-cultural samples and multiple adversarial research programs that were later integrated rather than one being falsified. That integration is a point in its favour and also a caution: adversarial collaboration produced a negotiated synthesis, not a decisive test.
strength.magnitude: Each dimension splits into two facets — ability and assertiveness (vertical), morality and friendliness (horizontal). Chawinwit & Koch (2026), across seven studies (N=4,577), found cluster analyses cleanly separated both the Big Two and the four facets, but the facet model did not fit better than the two-dimension model.
strength.boundaries: Not orthogonal (see the curvilinearity node). Not necessarily exhaustive (see ABC model). Warmth shows lower inter-perceiver consensus than agency. Most evidence is about perception of groups and strangers, not about intimate long-term relationships.

plain.what: People size each other up on two questions: are you warm, and are you capable. Warmth usually gets judged first.
plain.why: Nearly every influence, sales and charisma framework is a way of managing where you land on these two.
plain.catch: They are not independent dials, which breaks most of the advice built on them. See the next one.

body.def: Two dimensions summarise most social evaluation: a vertical dimension (agency, competence, status, assertiveness) and a horizontal one (communion, warmth, morality, friendliness). Proposed independently across several research programs, which were later negotiated into a shared Big Two framework.
body.mech: Warmth/communion is generally judged first and weighted more heavily; competence/agency second. The combination predicts the emotion a target evokes — warm+competent → admiration, cold+competent → envy, warm+incompetent → pity, cold+incompetent → contempt. The evolutionary rationale offered is that a social animal must first judge a stranger's intent, then their capacity to act on it.
body.intra: Your own self-evaluation splits the same way — how capable am I, and am I a good person. People typically self-enhance more on the warmth facets.
body.inter: You are placed somewhere in this space within seconds and the placement drives the emotion you evoke, not just the judgement.
body.app: Most influence and sales frameworks are toolkits for managing position on these two dimensions. v1 treated that as the master key. It is better described as the most reliable summary available, with the caveats above.

sources: Fiske, Cuddy & Glick (2007), Trends in Cognitive Sciences
Abele & Wojciszke (eds.) (2018), Agency and Communion in Social Psychology
Chawinwit & Koch (2026), Social Psychological and Personality Science, N=4,577
open: Whether the Big Two are a property of the social world or an artefact of how researchers ask the question. The data-driven challenge below is the sharpest version of that worry.

label: The axes are not orthogonal

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Published in Perspectives on Psychological Science as a synthesis across existing datasets rather than a single new experiment, which makes it robust to one lab's methods but dependent on the original data collections.
strength.magnitude: Demonstrated across one new and five previously published datasets, including a meta-analysis of the most comprehensive group-perception data collection available — 36 samples from more than 20 countries.
strength.boundaries: Established for perception of social groups. Whether the same curve governs perception of individuals in ongoing relationships is not established by this work.

plain.what: Push your competence signals very high and people start reading you as colder.
plain.why: It breaks the standard advice to maximise both warmth and authority at once.
plain.catch: The most impressive person in the room is often not the most liked. That is a measured pattern across 36 samples, not a saying.

body.def: Agency and communion are conventionally drawn as independent axes. They are not: perceived communion peaks at average agency and declines at both very low and very high agency.
body.mech: Four theoretical routes to the same prediction, including that extreme status implies competition and reduced shared interest. Entities read as very high-status are judged less warm, not equally warm.
body.intra: Your own bid for status has a ceiling past which it reads as coldness rather than capability.
body.inter: This is the empirical version of the folk observation that the most impressive person in the room is often not the most liked.
body.app: Directly contradicts advice to maximise authority and competence signalling. The target is not 'high on both' — it is calibrated agency with high communion. Any framework telling you to dominate the frame is trading warmth for status without saying so.

sources: Imhoff & Koch (2017), Perspectives on Psychological Science, 'How Orthogonal Are the Big Two of Social Perception?'
open: Where exactly the peak sits, and whether it moves with the perceiver's own status.

label: ABC model — agency, beliefs, communion

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The dispute was pursued through formal adversarial collaboration between the competing labs rather than duelling papers, which is unusually good practice and makes both sides' findings more credible.
strength.magnitude: Seven studies, total N=4,451. In the multidimensional scaling analysis, agency was the most differentiating dimension, beliefs second — and communion did not emerge as an independent dimension at all. A later adversarial collaboration (N=2,356, four continents) that included Fiske found lower perceiver consensus on warmth/communion than on agency or beliefs.
strength.boundaries: About stereotypes of societal groups, not individual impression formation. Its authors describe it as an extension of the two-dimension model rather than a replacement.

body.def: A data-driven challenge to the two-dimension consensus. When participants are allowed to generate and sort social groups without being constrained to warmth and competence, they organise primarily by agency/socioeconomic success, and second by conservative–progressive beliefs.
body.mech: The authors identify an empirical gap: the standard model constrains responses to two dimensions a priori, so finding two dimensions is partly guaranteed by the method. Removing the constraint changes the answer.
body.inter: Political and values alignment may do independent work in how you are categorised, separate from how warm or capable you seem.
body.app: If beliefs are a primary sorting dimension, then visible values alignment is not a warmth tactic — it is its own channel. No applied framework in this atlas treats it that way.

sources: Koch, Imhoff, Dotsch, Unkelbach & Alves (2016), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 110:675–709
Koch, Imhoff, Unkelbach, Nicolas, Fiske, Terache, Carrier & Yzerbyt (2020), Journal of Experimental Social Psychology — adversarial collaboration
open: Whether beliefs is a genuinely universal dimension or a feature of politically polarised societies. Cross-cultural testing is partial.

label: What heritability actually means

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The empirical regularity is among the most replicated in psychology. The interpretation is where the field's real disputes live.
strength.magnitude: Across the largest synthesis available — 2,748 publications, 17,804 traits, 14,558,903 twin pairs — reported heritability across all traits averages 49%. Estimates cluster strongly by functional domain rather than being uniform.
strength.boundaries: Four boundaries that almost every popular use of the word violates. It says nothing about an individual: there is no sense in which your own trait is 49% genetic. It says nothing about malleability: a highly heritable trait can be changed by an intervention nobody in the sample received. It is population-specific: reduce environmental variation and heritability rises mechanically, because the denominator shrinks. And it is not causation: it is a variance ratio, and the pathway can run through the environment.

plain.what: Heritability is a number about a group, not about you. It says how much of the variation between people lines up with genetic differences.
plain.why: It is the most misused statistic in psychology, wheeled out constantly to argue that change is impossible.
plain.catch: A high number does not mean fixed and says nothing about any individual. Improve everyone's environment and the number itself goes up, not down.

body.def: Heritability (h²) is the proportion of variance in a trait, within a particular population at a particular time, that is statistically associated with genetic variance in that population. It is a property of a population, not of a person or of a trait in the abstract.
body.mech: Estimated by comparing trait similarity across people of known genetic relatedness — identical versus fraternal twins, adoptees versus biological children — and partitioning variance into additive genetic (A), shared environment (C) and nonshared environment plus measurement error (E).
body.intra: A heritable trait is not a fixed trait. The number describes variation in a population you happen to be in, not a ceiling on you.
body.app: Heritability is routinely deployed to argue that an intervention is futile. That inference does not follow from the statistic, and the people making it usually know less about the statistic than they think.

sources: Polderman, Benyamin, de Leeuw, Sullivan, van Bochoven, Visscher & Posthuma (2015), Nature Genetics 47:702–709
open: Whether the additive-only model that fits most traits reflects biology or the limited power of twin designs to detect non-additive effects.

label: The classical twin design and its assumptions

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: This is a genuine, unresolved methodological dispute with serious people on both sides, not a fringe objection. A second known bias runs the other way: assortative mating violates the random-mating assumption and biases heritability downward, which is why some defenders argue the two errors partly cancel.
strength.magnitude: A comprehensive evaluation across 32 outcomes found the EEA was not strictly valid for most of them, but that violations significantly reduced heritability estimates in only one case (neuroticism). Simulation work modelling violated assumptions found large overestimation of heritability and underestimation of shared environment, including when gene–environment interaction was counted toward the genetic ground truth.
strength.boundaries: The strongest defence is convergence: adoption studies and twins-reared-apart designs, which do not rely on the EEA, give broadly similar answers. That is real evidence, though those designs carry their own selection problems.

body.def: The workhorse method: identical twins share ~100% of segregating genes, fraternal twins ~50%, and both types are assumed to share their environment to the same degree. Greater identical-twin similarity is then attributed to genes.
body.mech: The equal environments assumption (EEA) is what the inference rests on. If identical twins are also treated more alike — and they often are — then the extra similarity attributed to genes is partly environmental, and heritability is overestimated while shared environment is underestimated.
body.app: Every heritability figure in this layer inherits this uncertainty. Treat them as bounded estimates with a plausible upward bias, not measurements.

sources: Felson (2014), Social Science Research — comprehensive evaluation of the EEA across 32 outcomes
Simulation study of unmet twin-design assumptions (2020), bioRxiv preprint — not peer reviewed at time of retrieval
Sciencedirect overview of the equal environment assumption
open: How large the net bias is once EEA violation and assortative mating are both accounted for. Defenders and critics give very different answers and neither has settled it.

label: The laws of behaviour genetics

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The regularities themselves are about as replicated as anything in psychology. What they mean remains contested by the person who named them.
strength.magnitude: The second law is the one that surprises people most: across the largest twin synthesis, the data were inconsistent with substantial shared-environment influence for most traits. For cognitive ability, shared environment falls to roughly 0.10 by age 18–20 and stays there.
strength.boundaries: Turkheimer's own argument — frequently ignored by people who quote him — is that genes look like a more systematic source of variation than environment for methodological rather than substantive reasons. Development is nonlinear, interactive and hard to control experimentally; the twin design is a shortcut, and it does not show that genes are more fundamental than environments. At least one exception to the first law has been reported: beliefs about free will appear weakly or not at all heritable.

body.def: Four empirical regularities that summarise the field. First: all human behavioural traits are heritable. Second: the effect of being raised in the same family is smaller than the effect of genes. Third: a substantial portion of variation is accounted for by neither genes nor families. Fourth: a typical behavioural trait is associated with very many genetic variants, each accounting for a very small percentage of the variability.
body.mech: The first three map onto the A, C and E components of the twin model. The fourth was added from molecular data and explains both why candidate-gene studies failed to replicate and why genome-wide studies need enormous samples.
body.intra: 'The family you grew up in matters less than you think' is the accurate version. 'Parenting doesn't matter' is not — see gene–environment correlation.
body.app: Widely used to argue that upbringing is irrelevant. The third law says the largest single chunk of variance is explained by neither genes nor family, and we largely cannot say what it is.

sources: Turkheimer (2000), Current Directions in Psychological Science 9(5):160–164
Chabris, Lee, Cesarini, Benjamin & Laibson (2015), Current Directions in Psychological Science — the Fourth Law
Polderman et al. (2015), Nature Genetics
open: Whether law two survives better measurement of family environments, or whether shared environment is underestimated by how crudely it is measured.

label: Nonshared environment & the gloomy prospect

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The failure to find nonshared environmental predictors has itself replicated, which is the whole problem.
strength.magnitude: The E component typically carries a large share of variance, and it also contains all measurement error, which is rarely separated out.
strength.boundaries: If the gloomy prospect is right, a large portion of why people differ is not merely unmeasured but close to unmeasurable — chance events compounding over a life.

body.def: The largest environmental component of variance is nonshared — things that differ between siblings in the same family. The uncomfortable finding is that decades of work have failed to identify what it consists of.
body.mech: A quantitative review concluded that measured nonshared environmental variables do not account for a substantial portion of the nonshared variance that twin models say exists. Turkheimer's proposed reading — the 'gloomy prospect' — is that nonshared variance predominates not because of systematic effects of events siblings don't share, but because of the unsystematic effects of all environmental events, compounded by equally unsystematic processes that expose us to them.
body.intra: Some of why you are the way you are is contingency, not cause. That is not a comfortable finding and it is not a defeatist one.
body.app: Any framework claiming to explain a person's differences from their sibling by one identified factor is claiming to have solved something the field has not.

sources: Turkheimer & Waldron (2000), Psychological Bulletin 126(1):78 — quantitative review
Turkheimer (2000), Current Directions in Psychological Science
Plomin & Daniels (1987), the original formulation
open: Whether the nonshared variance is genuinely stochastic or merely badly measured. This is one of the most consequential open questions in the whole atlas.

label: Heritability rises with age

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Converges across twin studies, adoption studies and twins reared apart — three designs with different weaknesses.
strength.magnitude: Across six twin studies (about 11,000 pairs in four countries), heritability of general cognitive ability rose roughly linearly from ~41% at age 9 to ~55% at 12 to ~66% at 17. A meta-analysis of 23 longitudinal twin and adoption studies reports a rise from ~0.40 in early childhood to ~0.75–0.80 in adulthood. Reviewing twin, adoption and reared-apart designs, heritability reaches an asymptote near 0.80 at 18–20 and holds into adulthood, while shared environment falls to about 0.10 over the same span.
strength.boundaries: Stated explicitly by its reviewers: these conclusions apply to the Westernised industrial democracies where nearly all the studies were run. Whether the pattern holds elsewhere is unknown.

body.def: The heritability of cognitive ability increases across development rather than decreasing — the opposite of most people's intuition that environment accumulates.
body.mech: The leading explanation is gene–environment correlation: as people gain autonomy they increasingly select, modify and create environments matching their propensities, so early genetic differences get amplified by environmental feedback rather than washed out by it.
body.intra: The environments you choose as an adult amplify who you already were. That cuts both ways and is the strongest argument in this layer for deliberately choosing environments.
body.app: Often quoted as proving genetic determinism. The mechanism proposed is the opposite: it is environmental selection doing the amplifying.

sources: Haworth et al. (2010), Molecular Psychiatry 15:1112–1120 — ~11,000 twin pairs
Briley & Tucker-Drob (2013), Psychological Science 24(9):1704–1713 — 23 longitudinal studies
Bouchard (2013), Twin Research and Human Genetics 16(5):923–930 — the Wilson Effect review
open: Whether the same age-amplification holds outside Western industrialised populations.

label: Gene–environment correlation & genetic nurture

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Replicated in design as well as sample — non-transmitted-allele analyses and within-family polygenic comparisons are independent approaches that agree.
strength.magnitude: Using non-transmitted alleles in 21,637 individuals with at least one genotyped parent, the polygenic score computed from alleles the child did not inherit had an estimated effect on the child's educational attainment equal to 29.9% of the transmitted score's effect. Consistently, in a genome-wide study of ~3 million people, direct effects — controlling for parental scores — explained roughly half the polygenic index's total association with educational attainment. Notably, the same analysis found no comparable genetic-nurture effect for height and BMI: parental alleles predicted the child's body only insofar as the child inherited them.
strength.boundaries: That contrast matters. Genetic nurture is not a universal artefact; it appears for socially mediated outcomes like education and not for physically mediated ones like height.

body.def: Genes and environments are not independent. People inherit environments correlated with their genotype (passive), evoke responses from others (evocative), and select settings that fit them (active). The sharpest demonstration: parental genes that were never passed on still predict the child's outcomes.
body.mech: Parental genotype shapes the environment the parents build, which shapes the child — a causal path that runs through the environment but shows up in genetic analyses. This is 'genetic nurture'.
body.inter: Roughly half of what looks like inherited academic advantage is the environment that advantage built, transmitted socially.
body.app: This is the finding that breaks the clean nature/nurture partition, and it cuts against both camps. It undermines 'it's all genes' because half the signal runs through environments. It equally undermines naive parenting research, because parent–child similarity attributed to parenting is partly genetic transmission.

sources: Kong et al. (2018), Science 359:424–428 — non-transmitted alleles, N=21,637
Okbay et al. (2022), Nature Genetics 54:437–449 — direct effects roughly half the PGI association
Koellinger & Harden (2018), Science — accompanying perspective
open: How much of genetic nurture is parenting specifically versus neighbourhood, school and assortative mating.

label: Gene × environment interaction

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: Robustness checks including tests for publication bias and heterogeneity supported the pattern, and the result was not driven by a few large studies. Both the original proponent and his critics have publicly accepted the meta-analytic picture, which is unusually clean for a contested area.
strength.magnitude: A meta-analysis across 14 studies and 24,926 twin and sibling pairs from the United States, Australia, England, Sweden, Germany and the Netherlands found clear support for moderately sized Gene × SES effects in US studies — and effectively none in Western Europe and Australia, with the US/non-US difference itself statistically significant. In the Netherlands there was even a suggestion of the opposite pattern.
strength.boundaries: This is a cross-national moderator, not a universal law. The proposed explanation — that stronger social provision compresses environmental variation at the bottom, leaving no deprivation gradient for heritability to interact with — is a plausible inference, not a tested mechanism.

body.def: The hypothesis that genetic influence on a trait depends on the environment — specifically that genetic influences on cognitive ability are suppressed under socioeconomic deprivation and more fully expressed under advantage.
body.mech: If environments constrain the realisation of genetic potential, then heritability should be lower where deprivation is greater. The implication is that heritability is partly a readout of how equal a society is.
body.app: The single most important consequence in this layer: heritability is not a fixed biological constant. The same trait can be more or less heritable depending on the policy environment of the country you measure it in.

sources: Tucker-Drob & Bates (2016), Psychological Science 27(2):138–149 — meta-analysis, 24,926 pairs
Turkheimer, Haley, Waldron, D'Onofrio & Gottesman (2003), Psychological Science 14:623–628 — the original finding
open: Why the interaction is US-specific. Inequality is the obvious candidate but has not been directly tested as the moderator.

label: The candidate gene collapse

strength.label: failed
strength.replication: The pre-registration is what makes this decisive: the analyses were fixed before the data were seen, removing the flexibility that generated the original literature.
strength.magnitude: A pre-registered investigation identified the 18 candidate genes studied ten or more times and tested them across samples ranging from 62,138 to 443,264 individuals, drawing on UK Biobank, 23andMe and the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium — around 620,000 people in total. The 18 most-studied depression candidate genes were no more associated with depression than randomly chosen genes, and the gene-by-environment interaction hypotheses fared no better.
strength.boundaries: This does not mean depression is not heritable — twin-based heritability is around 37%. It means the heritability is spread across enormous numbers of variants with individually minuscule effects.

body.def: For roughly two decades, hundreds of studies reported that specific named genes — most famously a serotonin-transporter variant — predicted depression, sometimes in interaction with life stress. Essentially none of it held up.
body.mech: Small samples plus analytic flexibility plus publication bias produced a large literature of false positives. The Fourth Law explains why it was doomed: real effects of individual variants are far too small to detect in samples of a few hundred.
body.app: A whole generation of popular psychology built on 'the warrior gene', 'the depression gene' and similar. Treat any claim that a named single gene explains a psychological trait as false until shown otherwise.

sources: Border, Johnson, Evans, Smolen, Berley, Sullivan & Keller (2019), American Journal of Psychiatry 176(5):376–387
open: How much of the wider gene-by-environment interaction literature outside depression survives the same scrutiny.

label: Polygenic scores

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The predictive findings replicate well within-ancestry and the portability decay is itself predictable from population-genetic theory, which is unusually strong evidence that it is a real methodological limit rather than noise.
strength.magnitude: For educational attainment, a genome-wide study of ~3 million people produced an index explaining 12–16% of variance, with ~13% of variance in age-16 grade point average and ~8% in age-14 grade rank. Cognitive ability sits around 11%. That is well below the 50–80% twin heritability. Crucially, controlling for parental scores — the within-family estimate — roughly halves the association, because the between-family portion carries genetic nurture, assortative mating and population structure.
strength.boundaries: Portability is the hard limit. About 79% of participants in genome-wide studies are of European ancestry, and accuracy decays predictably with genetic distance from the training sample. The largest educational-attainment study of its time reported roughly 10.6% incremental variance explained in European-Americans but only 1.6% in African-Americans. For height, a UK-trained score explained ~11% in the UK and ~3% in a Japanese sample. Accuracy also varies within a single ancestry group by socioeconomic status, age and sex.

body.def: A single number summing the small estimated effects of many thousands of genetic variants, used to predict a trait. The replacement for candidate genes, and currently the strongest molecular prediction available for behavioural traits.
body.mech: Genome-wide association studies estimate tiny per-variant effects across millions of people; those weights are summed for an individual. The score predicts population variation, not individual outcomes.
body.intra: A score explaining 12% of population variance tells you very little about any individual, including you.
body.app: Being marketed for embryo selection and educational streaming. The within-family halving and the ancestry decay are the two facts that most such marketing omits.

sources: Okbay et al. (2022), Nature Genetics 54:437–449 — GWAS of ~3 million
Martin et al. (2019), Nature Genetics — portability and prediction disparities
Mostafavi, Harpak, Agarwal, Conley, Pritchard & Przeworski (2020), eLife — variable accuracy within an ancestry group
Ding et al. (2023) — accuracy across the genetic ancestry continuum
open: Whether scores trained on genuinely diverse samples close the portability gap, and whether within-family scores ever reach twin-study heritability.

label: The missing heritability gap

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The gap is observed consistently across traits and has been the field's central puzzle for over a decade.
strength.magnitude: For personality the gap is starker still. Twin studies put Big Five heritability at 40–60%, but a genome-wide analysis of 5,011 adults across 527,469 variants found significant common-variant heritability only for neuroticism (15%) and openness (21%), and none detectable for extraversion, agreeableness or conscientiousness.
strength.boundaries: The gap has narrowed as sample sizes have grown, which supports the 'many tiny effects' explanation over the 'twin estimates are wrong' explanation — but it has not closed.

body.def: Twin studies say cognitive ability is 50–80% heritable. Molecular scores built from measured DNA capture 11–16%. The difference is 'missing' in the sense that we have strong evidence it exists but cannot yet locate it in the genome.
body.mech: Candidate explanations include rare variants not captured by common-variant arrays, structural variation, gene–gene interaction, indirect genetic effects, and — the uncomfortable one — that twin estimates are inflated by violated assumptions.
body.app: Both camps mine this. Hereditarians point to the twin number, critics to the molecular one. The honest position is that the two methods disagree by a factor of three to five and nobody has fully explained why.

sources: Power & Pluess (2015), Translational Psychiatry 5:e604 — GREML on Big Five, N=5,011
Okbay et al. (2022), Nature Genetics
Polderman et al. (2015), Nature Genetics
open: This is the central unresolved question of the layer. Whichever way it resolves changes how every heritability figure in this atlas should be read.

label: Heritability of personality

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The meta-analytic estimate is stable. The design gap is the replication story: the method you choose roughly doubles or halves your answer.
strength.magnitude: A meta-analysis of 62 independent effect sizes representing over 100,000 participants of both sexes and all ages gives an average of .40 — 40% of individual differences associated with genetic variation, 60% with environmental. The conclusion survived correction for publication bias. Personality model and sex were not significant moderators.
strength.boundaries: Study design was a significant moderator, and this is the finding that matters most: twin studies gave .47, family and adoption studies gave .22 — less than half. Reanalysis of the same corpus found family resemblance of .54 for twins reared together, .45 for identical twins reared apart, and .26–.28 for other family aggregation.

body.def: How much of the variation in Big Five traits is associated with genetic variation — and how much the answer depends on which research design you use.
body.mech: Same variance-partitioning logic as any heritability estimate, applied to self-reported trait measures.
body.intra: Your personality is substantially but not overwhelmingly heritable, and the honest range is wide.
body.app: Commonly quoted as '40–60% heritable' from twin studies alone. The adoption-design figure of .22 belongs in the same sentence, and almost never appears in one.

sources: Vukasović & Bratko (2015) — meta-analysis, 62 effect sizes, >100,000 participants
Bratko, Butković & Vukasović Hlupić (2017), Psychological Topics 26(1) — reanalysis by family-member type
Power & Pluess (2015), Translational Psychiatry — molecular comparison
open: Why twin and adoption designs disagree so sharply. Candidate answers include EEA violation, restricted range in adoptive families, and age differences between the samples.

label: Wanting is not liking

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Built over three decades of converging rodent and human affective neuroscience, with the core dissociation holding across manipulations. The rodent work is the strong part; human evidence relies on implicit measures precisely because self-report conflates the two.
strength.magnitude: The dissociation is asymmetric by design: liking's neural substrate is described by its own researchers as small and fragile relative to wanting's. The clearest human case is drug tolerance, where motivation to take the drug grows even as the reported pleasure of a dose falls.
strength.boundaries: Two boundaries the popular version omits. First, wanting and liking are normally coherent — they come apart under specific manipulations, particularly dopaminergic ones, not as a routine condition. Second, subjective wanting and liking are hard to separate by self-report, partly because people lack direct access to the underlying processes and partly because they try to keep their answers internally consistent: having said they want something, they infer that they must like it.

plain.what: Your brain runs chasing something and enjoying it on two different systems, and they can come apart.
plain.why: It explains how you can compulsively want something you have stopped actually enjoying.
plain.catch: Wanting runs on a large, easily triggered system; liking on a small, fragile one. Anything built to hook you aims at the first and ignores the second.

body.def: Reward decomposes into at least two dissociable components with separable neural substrates. 'Wanting' — incentive salience, the motivational pull toward a reward and its cues — is generated by large, robust mesolimbic dopamine systems. 'Liking' — the actual hedonic impact when the reward arrives — is mediated by much smaller, fragile opioid and endocannabinoid 'hedonic hotspots' and is not dopamine-dependent.
body.mech: Dopamine manipulations amplify or abolish wanting while leaving liking reactions intact, measured in animals by stereotyped orofacial affective responses to taste. Because wanting is generated by systems that are more numerous, more diverse and more easily activated than those for liking, the two can come apart — and wanting can be driven up without any corresponding increase in pleasure.
body.intra: Craving is not evidence of anticipated pleasure. The strength of a pull tells you about one system, and it is not the system that determines whether the thing will be good when you get it.
body.app: Every engagement-optimised product is a wanting machine. Optimising for pull and optimising for satisfaction are separable targets, and the first is far easier to hit.

sources: Berridge & Robinson (1998), Brain Research Reviews 28(3):309–369
Berridge, Robinson & Aldridge (2009), Current Opinion in Pharmacology 9(1):65–73
Berridge (2007), Psychopharmacology — debate over dopamine and incentive salience
Berridge & Kringelbach (2015), Pleasure systems in the brain
open: How far the rodent-derived dissociation transfers to human subjective experience, where the two are much harder to measure apart.

label: Reward prediction error

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: This is an active, unresolved dispute in a live field. One camp argues the concept survives if suitably modified and generalised; the other argues that some findings demand fundamentally different explanations. A 2024 Nature Neuroscience perspective concludes a complete account will probably need to move beyond the reward prediction error hypothesis while retaining its core explanatory power. That is a fair summary of where it stands.
strength.magnitude: Its explanatory success is real and its proponents have refined rather than abandoned it, incorporating sensory prediction error, distributional encoding and belief states.
strength.boundaries: The account has been under increasing strain. It did not predict several striking effects: dopamine firing increasing during delay under uncertainty, dopamine ramps in spatial tasks, dopamine waves, and substantial heterogeneity of responses across neurons and brain regions. Dopamine projections to regions beyond the nucleus accumbens can show activity that does not fit the prediction-error model at all. And there is a persistent movement problem: signals in dopamine neurons projecting to dorsomedial striatum are modulated by choice direction in a way distinct from prediction error, implying movement encoding rather than an action-specific error signal.

body.def: The dominant computational account: dopamine neurons signal the difference between predicted and received reward, providing a training signal that drives learning. Proposed in 1997 and one of the genuine triumphs of computational neuroscience for its fit with temporal-difference reinforcement learning.
body.mech: A positive error when outcomes beat prediction, a dip when they fall short, and — once a cue reliably predicts reward — a shift of the signal from the reward to the cue.
body.app: Popularly rendered as 'dopamine is the surprise chemical' or 'your brain rewards the unexpected'. The finding is real and narrower than that, and the field is currently arguing about how much of dopamine's function it covers.

sources: Schultz, Dayan & Montague (1997) — the original proposal
Explaining dopamine through prediction errors and beyond (2024), Nature Neuroscience — perspective on where the evidence succeeds and falls short
Reward prediction error does not explain movement selectivity in DMS-projecting dopamine neurons (2019), eLife
Dopamine, Updated: Reward Prediction Error and Beyond (2020), Current Opinion in Neurobiology
open: Whether dopamine heterogeneity across neurons and projection targets can be accommodated inside a generalised prediction-error framework, or whether it requires a different theory.

label: Dopamine is not the pleasure chemical

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: This is one of the more secure claims in the atlas precisely because it survives the disagreement between the field's two dominant theories.
strength.magnitude: Both major theoretical camps agree on this point despite disagreeing about almost everything else. Incentive-salience theory and prediction-error theory are rival accounts of what dopamine does — neither holds that it encodes pleasure.
strength.boundaries: Not that dopamine is unrelated to reward — it is central to it. The error is the specific equation of dopamine with felt pleasure.

body.def: The single most widespread neuroscience misconception in popular psychology. Dopamine does not mediate the hedonic impact of reward. It is heavily involved in motivation, prediction and movement — not in how good the reward feels when it arrives.
body.mech: The hedonic impact of reward is mediated by opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots, not by dopamine. Dopamine depletion in animals abolishes pursuit of a reward without abolishing the pleasure reaction to it.
body.intra: 'Dopamine hit', 'dopamine detox' and 'dopamine fasting' are all built on the wrong premise. If a behaviour has you in its grip, the relevant system is wanting, and turning down pleasure will not touch it.
body.app: A commercial folk-neuroscience industry rests on this misconception. It is a useful diagnostic: if a source calls dopamine the pleasure chemical, it has not read the primary literature.

sources: Berridge & Robinson (1998), Brain Research Reviews 28(3):309–369
Berridge, Robinson & Aldridge (2009), Current Opinion in Pharmacology

label: Incentive sensitization

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: The neural sensitization findings are robust in animals. The translation to human addiction remains a theoretical framework competing with others rather than a settled account, which is why this node is graded moderate while the underlying wanting/liking dissociation is graded solid.
strength.magnitude: Thirty years of development and a substantial rodent literature behind the sensitization claim.
strength.boundaries: 'In vulnerable individuals' is doing real work in the theory and the vulnerability is not well specified. The extension from drugs to behavioural compulsions is a proposal rather than an established finding.

body.def: A theory of addiction built from three components: repeated intermittent exposure to addictive drugs produces mesolimbic sensitization in vulnerable individuals; once induced, that sensitization is very persistent, lasting long after use stops; and dopamine's role in reward is to mediate wanting rather than liking. It follows that with repeated exposure, wanting escalates while liking does not.
body.mech: Sensitized wanting becomes narrowly focused on the drug through associative pairing of cues with use, so cues capture attention and provoke urges out of proportion to any pleasure obtained. The theory is claimed to extend beyond drugs to food bingeing, gambling and other compulsive behaviours.
body.app: It explains a real and otherwise puzzling clinical observation: people continuing to pursue something that has stopped giving them pleasure. That pattern is not weakness of will and it is not a search for pleasure.

sources: Robinson & Berridge (1993), Brain Research Reviews 18:291
Robinson & Berridge (2025), Annual Review of Psychology — the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction 30 years on
open: What constitutes the 'vulnerability' the theory requires, and whether behavioural addictions genuinely share the mechanism.

label: Is addiction a brain disease?

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: Notably, Berridge — whose incentive-sensitization work is often cited by both camps — takes a middle position: the neural changes are extreme enough to be viewed as pathological, the disease label is not unreasonable and deserves tolerating, but most people with addiction should not be considered significantly brain damaged.
strength.magnitude: The critics' strongest empirical card is natural remission. High rates of recovery in community samples — one review reporting that on average over half of people with alcohol or other drug addiction recover, and a Canadian survey in which around half reported achieving stable recovery at their first attempt — sit awkwardly with 'chronic and relapsing'. Defenders reply that high natural-recovery rates are compatible with the model and that many attempts typically precede success.
strength.boundaries: This is genuinely unresolved and both sides include serious researchers. A 2014 Nature editorial asserting the chronic-relapsing-brain-disease view as uncontroversial among scientists drew a protest letter signed by 94 addiction scholars and researchers. Defenders counter that denying the brain-disease framing reduces access to healthcare and treatment, with severe consequences.

body.def: An active dispute about what kind of thing addiction is. The brain disease model holds it is a chronic, relapsing brain disease produced by prolonged drug effects on the brain. Critics argue the neurobiological changes are real but better understood as deeply entrenched learning and development, not irreversible pathology.
body.mech: Both sides accept that the brain changes. The disagreement is whether those changes constitute a disease or a state of profound, context-sensitive neuroplasticity that can adapt again.
body.app: The practical stake is not academic. The model shapes treatment funding, legal responsibility, stigma and whether a person believes recovery is available to them. Evidence is also mixed on whether the disease framing reduces stigma, which was one of its original justifications.

sources: Leshner (1997) — the original chronic-relapsing-brain-disease claim
Heather, Best, Kawalek, Field, Lewis, Rotgers et al. (2018), Addiction Research & Theory 26:249–255 — Addiction Theory Network launch
Lewis (2017), Neuroethics 10:7–18 — addiction and the brain: development, not disease
Heilig et al. (2021), Neuropsychopharmacology — addiction as a brain disease revised
Hall, Carter & Forlini (2015), Lancet Psychiatry 2:105–110
open: Whether the dispute is empirical at all, or a disagreement about what 'disease' should mean. Several participants argue the latter.

label: Habit formation

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: The asymptotic-curve finding at the individual level was itself the contribution — prior work had shown it only for group averages. The specific 66-day figure has not been established as a general constant and the study does not claim it is one.
strength.magnitude: 96 volunteers chose a daily eating, drinking or activity behaviour and rated automaticity daily for 84 days. Median time to reach 95% of asymptotic automaticity was 66 days, with a range of 18 to 254 days — the slowest taking roughly fourteen times longer than the fastest.
strength.boundaries: The headline number is far weaker than its use implies. 82 of 96 provided analysable data; the model fitted for 62, of whom only 39 showed a good fit — so the median comes from a subset, not the sample. For many participants the asymptote was a projection beyond the 84-day observation window. The behaviours were simple ones in stable contexts; for exercise the median was around 91 days. And the outcome was self-reported automaticity, not habit in the strict behavioural sense.

body.def: How repeated behaviour in a consistent context becomes automatic. The source of the ubiquitous '66 days to form a habit' claim — and a good case study in how a careful finding becomes a slogan.
body.mech: With repetition in a stable context, self-reported automaticity increases along an asymptotic curve, rising fastest early and flattening. Missing a single opportunity did not materially affect the process, which is the study's most practically useful and least quoted finding.
body.intra: The usable findings are the opposite of the slogan: there is no universal number, variation is enormous, complexity slows it sharply, and one missed day does not reset anything.
body.app: '21 days' is a misreading of a 1960 book about plastic-surgery patients adjusting psychologically — never a habit study. '66 days' is at least from a habit study, but it is a median drawn from under half the participants. Both are quoted as laws.

sources: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle (2010), European Journal of Social Psychology 40(6):998–1009
Verplanken & Orbell (2003), Journal of Applied Social Psychology — the Self-Report Habit Index used to measure it
open: Whether automaticity as self-reported corresponds to habit as behavioural scientists define it — insensitivity to outcome devaluation. These are not the same construct and the popular literature treats them as one.

label: What emotions are — the live dispute

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: This is not a replication failure; it is a genuine theoretical dispute among productive research programmes, each with substantial evidence. Any source presenting one account as settled is misrepresenting the field.
strength.magnitude: A third position has grown from large-scale data-driven work: semantic space theory, which argues emotion is high-dimensional, defined by blends of upward of 20 distinct kinds, with fuzzy rather than sharp boundaries — contradicting basic emotion theory's discrete categories and constructionism's reduction to low-dimensional valence and arousal simultaneously. On that account emotion concepts like 'anger' are primary in how experience unfolds, more so than core affect.
strength.boundaries: The field is described in its own literature as enduringly fragmented: emotions are variously conceptualised as innate responses, mental constructs, cognitive appraisals, or self-organising dynamic states, and the fragmentation is attributed partly to narrow methods.

body.def: The central unresolved question of the field. Basic emotion theory holds there are a limited number of discrete, evolved emotion kinds with characteristic expressions and physiology. Constructionist accounts hold that emotions are constructed in the moment from general-purpose ingredients — core affect plus concepts plus context — so 'anger' is a category people apply rather than a natural kind with a fixed signature.
body.mech: The disagreement is not about whether emotions are real. It is about whether discrete emotion categories carve nature at its joints or are learned concepts imposed on continuously varying affective states.
body.intra: If the constructionist account is even partly right, your emotional vocabulary is not a description of your states but part of what produces them.
body.inter: You are not reading emotions off people. You are inferring them, using your own concepts, from movement plus context.
body.app: Emotion-recognition products, affect-detection hiring tools and lie-detection protocols assume the strong version of basic emotion theory. That assumption is exactly what is disputed.

sources: Barrett, Adolphs, Marsella, Martinez & Pollak (2019), Psychological Science in the Public Interest 20(1):1–68
Keltner, Brooks & Cowen (2023), Current Directions in Psychological Science — semantic space theory
Cowen & Keltner (2018), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 22(4):274–276 — response to Barrett and colleagues
Ekman & Cordaro (2011), Emotion Review — what is meant by calling emotions basic
open: Whether the dispute is resolvable with current methods at all. Several participants argue the fragmentation stems from methodological narrowness rather than from the phenomenon.

label: Are facial expressions universal?

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: The small-scale-society findings replicate across Himba, Hadza, Trobriand and Mwani samples and across free-sort, free-label, word-matching and choice-from-array methods. The large-scale machine-learning finding is newer and has not been independently replicated. Both are in this node because both exist.
strength.magnitude: Himba participants in Namibia, without cues to emotion concepts, did not produce the presumed universal sorting pattern while US participants did. Himba, Hadza and Trobriand participants presented with the standard facial poses rarely offered the predicted emotion labels spontaneously, instead using action identifications like 'crying', 'laughing', 'looking'. A wide-eyed gasping face read as fear in Western samples was identified by a large majority of Trobrianders as a threat display.
strength.boundaries: The counter-evidence is serious and recent. Applying deep neural networks to 6 million videos from 144 countries, one study found 16 facial expression types occurred systematically in specific contexts — weddings, sporting competitions, fireworks — with those context associations about 70% preserved across 12 world regions. That is a genuinely different kind of evidence: naturalistic production at scale rather than laboratory recognition.

body.def: The common view — that a person's emotional state can be read off their facial movements — underpins legal judgments, security protocols, psychiatric diagnosis, hiring tools and commercial emotion-recognition software. A major review concluded the evidence does not support it in that strong form.
body.mech: The critical original tests of universality were run between 1969 and 1975 in small-scale societies using methods that supplied participants with emotion words or forced choice from a short list. When tasks are made less constrained — free sorting, free labelling, controlling for valence differences between targets and foils — support weakens considerably.
body.inter: Your confidence that you can read someone's face is partly a product of sharing their cultural context. Across contexts, the signal degrades faster than the confidence does.
body.app: The practical stake is large: commercial emotion-recognition deployed in hiring, security and policing rests on the contested strong claim. A smile may signal submission rather than happiness.

sources: Barrett, Adolphs, Marsella, Martinez & Pollak (2019), Psychological Science in the Public Interest 20(1):1–68
Gendron, Roberson, van der Vyver & Barrett (2014), Emotion 14(2):251–262 — Himba free-sort
Gendron, Crivelli & Barrett (2018), Current Directions in Psychological Science — universality reconsidered
Crivelli, Russell, Jarillo & Fernández-Dols (2017) — Trobriand free-labelling
Cowen, Keltner, Schroff, Jou, Adam & Prasad (2021), Nature 589:251–257 — 16 expressions across 144 countries
open: Whether naturalistic production at scale and constrained laboratory recognition are even measuring the same thing. The two literatures currently talk past each other.

label: Valence and arousal — the agreed floor

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: This is the one part of the emotion-perception literature both camps accept, which makes it the most secure claim in this layer.
strength.magnitude: Himba, Trobriand and Hadza participants rarely confused normatively pleasant and unpleasant facial poses across free-sorting, free-labelling, word-matching and choice-from-array tasks. Trobrianders rated valence and arousal in photos of spontaneous expressions from another Papua New Guinean society and their ratings largely agreed with US raters.
strength.boundaries: 'Minimal' is the operative word. Knowing someone feels bad and is activated does not tell you whether they are angry, afraid or in pain — and those call for opposite responses.

body.def: Beneath the dispute there is a settled finding. Pleasantness–unpleasantness (valence) and high–low activation (arousal) are consistently perceived in facial movements across both industrialised and small-scale societies. This is sometimes called minimal universality.
body.mech: Whatever else a face conveys, it reliably conveys whether the person is feeling good or bad and how activated they are. Discrete category assignment is what varies.
body.intra: Valence and arousal are also the two dimensions along which your own affective state is most reliably reportable. Anything finer is interpretation.
body.inter: You can trust your read of whether someone is positive or negative and how activated. Treat the specific category as a hypothesis to check, not a perception.
body.app: This is the defensible version of reading a room: register valence and arousal, then ask rather than assume which emotion it is.

sources: Gendron, Crivelli & Barrett (2018), Current Directions in Psychological Science
Russell (2003) — core affect and minimal universality
Gendron et al. (2014), Emotion; Crivelli et al. (2016; 2017)
open: Whether valence and arousal are two dimensions or whether dominance is a genuine third — the older dimensional literature proposed three.

label: Interoception

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: The three-dimensional structure is widely adopted and its authors themselves have proposed it needs revision. Interoceptive differences are associated with a long list of conditions, but most of that evidence is correlational.
strength.magnitude: The construct is standardly divided into three dimensions: accuracy (objective ability to detect internal signals, typically via heartbeat detection), sensibility (self-reported tendency to attend to bodily sensations), and metacognitive awareness (correspondence between actual performance and confidence in it).
strength.boundaries: The critical and frequently ignored finding: the association between these three dimensions is weak or non-existent. People who believe they are attuned to their bodies are not reliably the people who can actually detect their heartbeats. There is also unresolved inconsistency about which questionnaires even measure sensibility.

body.def: The sensing of signals about the internal state of the body — heartbeat, breathing, visceral state — and its proposed contribution to emotional experience.
body.mech: Bodily afferents reach brainstem structures and are relayed to the thalamus, insula and somatosensory cortices. Constructionist accounts of emotion lean heavily on interoceptive signal as the raw affective ingredient that concepts then categorise.
body.intra: 'Listen to your body' assumes accuracy and sensibility go together. They largely do not, so confidence in your bodily read is a poor guide to its accuracy.
body.app: Interoception-based interventions are proliferating. The evidence base is largely correlational and the biofeedback intervention findings are described in the literature as mixed.

sources: Garfinkel, Seth, Barrett, Suzuki & Critchley (2015) — three-dimensional model
Garfinkel et al. (2016), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 371(1708):20160014
Khalsa et al. (2018) — interoception consensus paper
Murphy, Brewer, Catmur & Bird (2019) — critique proposing revision of the three-dimensional model
open: Whether interoceptive accuracy as measured by heartbeat tasks generalises to other bodily axes at all, and whether the construct is measuring one thing.

label: Affective forecasting & impact bias

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: Live dispute. Wilson and Gilbert published a direct reply titled 'The Impact Bias Is Alive and Well', disputing how the critics computed effect sizes from specific studies. Subsequent work refines rather than resolves: people appear better at predicting the intensity of feeling about an event than at predicting how frequently they will feel it afterwards or its effect on their general mood — so the original construct may have conflated distinguishable things.
strength.magnitude: Demonstrated across student samples, sports fans and voters. Effects reported as more pronounced for negative events, which one explanation attributes to neglecting one's own coping capacity.
strength.boundaries: A serious methodological challenge: people may accurately predict their feelings about an event while overestimating their feelings in general — and the standard procedure asks them to predict one and later report the other. Under that account participants forecast accurately when the question is clarified, and much of the bias is a procedural artifact of a mismatched question.

body.def: The claim that people systematically overestimate how intensely and how long future events will affect them emotionally — originally the durability bias, later broadened to impact bias when it appeared initial reactions were mispredicted too.
body.mech: Two proposed mechanisms: focalism, where attention fixes on the focal event and ignores everything else that will also be happening; and adaptation neglect, failing to anticipate your own coping.
body.intra: The usable residue survives the dispute: you will think about a future event less often than you expect, and other things will be happening. Whether the intensity prediction is wrong is genuinely unsettled.
body.app: Heavily used in decision advice — 'you'll get over it faster than you think'. That is the durability claim, which is in better shape than the intensity claim.

sources: Gilbert, Pinel, Wilson, Blumberg & Wheatley (1998) — durability bias
Levine, Lench, Kaplan & Safer (2012), JPSP — accuracy and artifact, including a meta-analysis of forecasting research
Wilson & Gilbert (2013), JPSP — 'The Impact Bias Is Alive and Well'
Lench, Levine, Perez et al. (2019), JPSP — intensity versus frequency versus mood effects
open: Whether the bias survives once the forecasting question is disambiguated. The two camps computed effect sizes from the same studies and got different answers, which suggests the dispute is partly about coding decisions.

label: Does the Big Five hold everywhere?

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: This is a single society and it is one study, which is the honest limit on how far it should be pushed. But it is a direct test of a universality claim in exactly the population the claim had never been tested in, and it failed comprehensively rather than marginally.
strength.magnitude: Tsimane forager–horticulturalists in Bolivia (n=632) completed a translated 44-item Big Five Inventory administered verbally by a trained bilingual Tsimane interviewer. Support failed on all five tests attempted: internal consistency, response stability, external validity against observed behaviour, exploratory and confirmatory factor structure, and Procrustes rotation against a US target. No Big Five scale reached the conventional .70 internal-reliability threshold, and average congruence with the US structure was .62 against a .90 benchmark. A separate sample of 430 Tsimane rating their spouses did not improve it.
strength.boundaries: The authors worked hard to break their own result and could not. Stratifying by education, Spanish fluency, sex and age made no difference; removing items with extreme response distributions did not improve fit; correcting for acquiescence bias did not improve reliability. What emerged instead was two well-defined factors, which the authors suggest may reflect socioecological features common to small-scale societies.

body.def: The five-factor structure has been recovered across many societies, which is usually taken to show it is a human universal. Almost all of those societies were literate and urban. The first test in a largely illiterate indigenous society did not find it.
body.mech: If the five factors are a property of human personality, they should emerge from trait ratings anywhere. If they are partly a property of how literate, schooled populations use trait language, they should not.
body.app: Personality instruments are exported globally on the assumption the structure travels. In the one population most unlike the samples the instruments were built on, it did not.

sources: Gurven, von Rueden, Massenkoff, Kaplan & Lero Vie (2013), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 104(2):354–370
open: Whether the two-factor Tsimane structure appears in other small-scale societies, and whether it corresponds to anything in the industrialised five.

label: HEXACO and the sixth factor

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Six factors have been recovered repeatedly across unrelated languages, which is stronger evidence than recovery within one language family. Honesty-Humility shows incremental validity over cognitive ability and the Big Five for workplace delinquency and integrity outcomes.
strength.magnitude: It was not invented from theory. A Korean lexical study turned up a clearly interpretable sixth factor, and a large-scale reanalysis of eight lexical studies across seven languages — Dutch, French, German, Hungarian, Italian, Korean and Polish — found six factors emerging consistently rather than five. The sixth factor explained Machiavellianism and psychopathy, and prosocial traits like morality and cooperation, better than the lexical Big Five did.
strength.boundaries: The obvious objection is that Honesty-Humility is just the high end of Agreeableness renamed. The answer is empirical: lexical Honesty-Humility was largely unrelated to Big Five markers, though substantially correlated with the five-factor model's Agreeableness domain — specifically its Straightforwardness and Modesty facets, which are themselves only weakly correlated with the lexical Big Five version of Agreeableness. Realigning the facets to produce separate factors improved prediction of deceit-without-hostility traits.

body.def: A six-factor alternative to the Big Five: Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Openness. It keeps three factors largely intact, rotates Agreeableness and Emotionality so that anger sits with low Agreeableness rather than with Neuroticism, and adds a sixth factor the Big Five does not contain.
body.mech: Honesty-Humility contrasts sincerity, fairness, greed-avoidance and modesty against boastfulness, hypocrisy, greed and untruthfulness. Its authors describe it as individual differences in reluctance versus willingness to exploit others.
body.inter: The trait that predicts whether someone will exploit you when they can is the one the dominant personality model omits.
body.app: Directly relevant to selection and to the dark-triad layer: none of the lexical Big Five factors correlated significantly with Machiavellianism, primary psychopathy or social adroitness, while Honesty-Humility did strongly and negatively.

sources: Ashton, Lee, Perugini, Szarota, de Vries, Di Blas et al. (2004) — six-factor solutions from psycholexical studies in seven languages
Ashton & Lee (2007), Personality and Social Psychology Review 11:150–166
Ashton & Lee (2005), Journal of Personality 73 — Honesty-Humility, the Big Five, and the five-factor model
Lee, Ashton & Shin (2005), Human Performance 18(2) — workplace delinquency and integrity
Hahn, Lee & Ashton (1999) — the Korean lexical study
open: Whether six is the ceiling. The same lexical logic that produced a sixth factor has been used to argue for seven in some languages.

label: Can personality change?

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Large evidence base and effects that persisted past the intervention window, which is the part that matters — short-term change that reverts is not trait change.
strength.magnitude: 207 studies tracking personality trait measures during interventions, including true experiments and pre-post designs. Interventions were associated with changes over an average of 24 weeks at around d = .37. The increases replicated across experimental and non-experimental designs and for non-clinical interventions, and persisted in longitudinal follow-ups beyond the intervention period.
strength.boundaries: Emotional stability was the primary domain that changed, followed by extraversion — so 'personality changes' is really 'neuroticism moves, and to a lesser degree extraversion'. Patients presenting with anxiety disorders changed most; those treated for substance use changed least. The type of therapy was not strongly associated with the amount of change, which is itself informative: it suggests something general rather than any specific technique.

body.def: Traits are usually described as stable. A meta-analysis of intervention studies found they move measurably, and faster than the stability framing implies.
body.mech: Most claims about trait stability come from passive longitudinal studies, which observe people who are not being intervened on. Intervention studies ask a different question.
body.intra: The defensible claim is that the trait most amenable to change is the one most associated with distress, and that roughly six months of structured intervention is the timescale. Not 'you can become anyone'.
body.app: Personal-development marketing claims trait change on far thinner evidence and far shorter timescales. This is the actual number.

sources: Roberts, Luo, Briley, Chow, Su & Hill (2017), Psychological Bulletin 143(2):117–141
open: Whether change generalises outside clinical and structured contexts, and how much of the measured change is trait change versus state change captured by trait questionnaires.

label: The person–situation debate

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The density-distribution result has been examined across multiple experience-sampling studies and a meta-analysis, and Mischel himself later retracted some of the original claims.
strength.magnitude: The resolution is not that one side won. Fleeson's density-distribution finding reframed the question: individual behaviour varies substantially across situations around a person-specific mean, and those behavioural states aggregate over time into distributions that are themselves stable and person-distinguishing. So both observations were correct — behaviour really is highly variable moment to moment, and people really do differ stably in their distributions.
strength.boundaries: Whole trait theory formalises this by splitting traits into a descriptive side (the density distribution of states) and an explanatory side (social-cognitive mechanisms that produce those states). Critics note the Big Five describes the first and has historically been thin on the second.

body.def: The foundational argument about whether behaviour is driven by stable traits or by situations. Mischel's 1968 book argued that behaviour is too cross-situationally inconsistent for trait concepts to be tenable, and that validity coefficients of about r = .30 — the 'personality coefficient' — were useless for predicting individual behaviour.
body.mech: The charge had real force: trait theory predicts consistency and what is typically observed is inconsistency. Its impact was severe enough that many personality psychologists began doubting the entire enterprise.
body.intra: You are not one setting on a dial. You are a distribution, and you spend time across much of your own range — which is why 'am I an introvert' is a badly formed question.
body.inter: Judging someone from one situation samples one point from a distribution you have not seen the shape of.
body.app: Trait-based selection and profiling assume the mean predicts the instance. It predicts the distribution. That is a weaker and more honest claim.

sources: Mischel (1968), Personality and Assessment
Fleeson (2001), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 80(6):1011–1027 — traits as density distributions of states
Fleeson & Gallagher (2009), JPSP 97(6):1097–1114 — fifteen experience-sampling studies and a meta-analysis
Fleeson & Jayawickreme (2015), Journal of Research in Personality 56:82–92 — whole trait theory
open: Whether the social-cognitive mechanisms that produce trait states can be identified specifically enough to be useful. That is whole trait theory's own stated agenda, not an achievement.

label: The dark triad — three traits or one?

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: The overlap finding replicates across research groups, including groups on both sides of the dispute. What is contested is the interpretation — whether a latent correlation of −.95 means one construct measured twice, or two constructs that happen to covary almost completely.
strength.magnitude: Using meta-analytic estimates from self-report data (N=1,402, k=4), the latent dark triad factor and low Honesty-Humility showed a latent correlation of −0.95 — near-complete overlap. Low Honesty-Humility is repeatedly the strongest basic-personality predictor of the dark triad traits, with up to 90% shared variance, and predicts them more strongly than five-factor Agreeableness does.
strength.boundaries: That result is what drives the harder conclusion in the literature: that the dark triad concept is largely redundant and adds little to traditional personality models. It is not unopposed. A 2021 paper argues for theoretical and empirical dissociations between the dark factor of personality and low Honesty-Humility, and a 2022 paper makes the case that the two are nearly perfectly correlated and distinct constructs, using differing relations with revengefulness as the proof.

plain.what: Narcissism, manipulativeness and callousness, grouped together as a dark cluster.
plain.why: It is the most popular idea in pop psychology about difficult people.
plain.catch: It is genuinely unsettled whether these are three things or one thing wearing three names, and that changes what any of it predicts.

body.def: Narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy, grouped in 2002 as three traits sharing a tendency to be callous, selfish and manipulative. The live question is whether the shared variance between them is a distinct thing at all, or simply the low end of a personality dimension already in the standard models.
body.mech: If the three correlate because they share a common core, that core needs a name and a location in personality space. The strongest candidate is the low pole of HEXACO Honesty-Humility — sincerity, fairness, greed-avoidance and modesty, inverted.
body.inter: The practically useful version does not depend on the dispute: there is a single dimension running from sincere-and-fair to exploitative, it is measurable, and it is the best available predictor of whether someone will take advantage of you when they can.
body.app: An enormous popular literature treats the three as separate diagnosable types. The evidence better supports one dimension with different surface presentations — and that dimension was already in the six-factor personality model before the dark triad was named.

sources: Paulhus & Williams (2002) — the original grouping
Hodson, Book, Visser, Volk, Ashton & Lee (2018), Journal of Research in Personality 73:123–129 — latent correlation −0.95
Horsten, Moshagen, Zettler & Hilbig (2021), Journal of Research in Personality 95:104154 — dissociations between the dark factor and low Honesty-Humility
Muris, Merckelbach, Otgaar & Meijer (2017) — meta-analysis of the shared core
open: Whether a latent correlation of −.95 leaves enough residual variance to be theoretically meaningful. Both camps agree on the number and disagree on what it implies.

label: Narcissism — grandiose and vulnerable

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The trifurcated and narcissism-spectrum models are described in the literature as the current state of the art and are broadly convergent, which is more agreement than most disputes in this atlas enjoy.
strength.magnitude: The two presentations are weakly related or uncorrelated in the general population, depending on the measure — which is remarkable for two things sharing a construct label. The relationship is also non-linear: they are distinct traits at lower levels of grandiosity and blend into an antagonistic core at higher levels, so the more grandiose someone is, the more vulnerability travels with it.
strength.boundaries: Vulnerable narcissism is largely divergent from both grandiose narcissism and clinical narcissistic personality disorder. Childhood abuse relates significantly to vulnerable but not grandiose narcissism. Clinically, the neurotic and antagonistic aspects carry the relevant outcomes — grandiose narcissism specifically was not correlated with several measures of impaired wellbeing.

body.def: Two presentations that share a name and much less else. Grandiose narcissism involves arrogance, superiority, attention-seeking and self-promotion. Vulnerable narcissism involves low self-esteem, hypersensitivity, and internalising distress.
body.mech: The trifurcated model resolves the puzzle by splitting narcissism into three personality dimensions: agentic extraversion, antagonism, and neuroticism. Antagonism is the shared core of both presentations. Grandiosity adds agentic extraversion; vulnerability adds neuroticism.
body.inter: The everyday use of 'narcissist' almost always means the grandiose presentation, which is the one least associated with distress and most associated with charm at first meeting. The vulnerable presentation looks nothing like the stereotype.
body.app: Narcissism was the largest unique predictor of counterproductive work behaviour among the dark traits after controlling for the Big Five. But which narcissism is being measured changes what the finding means.

sources: Miller, Lynam, Hyatt & Campbell (2017) and Miller et al. (2016) — the trifurcated model
Krizan & Herlache (2018) — narcissism spectrum model
Jauk, Weigle, Lehmann, Benedek & Neubauer (2017); Jauk et al. (2018), Frontiers in Psychology 9:1305 — non-linear association
Kaufman, Weiss, Miller & Campbell (2018), Journal of Personality Disorders 32 — clinical correlates
Weiss, Campbell, Lynam & Miller (2019), The Handbook of Antagonism
open: Whether grandiose and vulnerable narcissism should share a construct name at all given how weakly they correlate.

label: Psychopathy and the boldness dispute

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: Whether self-report scores reflect the same underlying construct as the clinical checklist is described in the literature as an important open concern rather than a settled matter. One review concludes a leading self-report triarchic measure is not yet a contender to replace the checklist.
strength.magnitude: The live dispute is whether boldness belongs in psychopathy at all, since it includes seemingly adaptive traits. In a sample of 1,565 adult offenders, boldness added incremental validity in predicting the checklist's representation of psychopathy, especially its interpersonal traits — superficial charm, deceitfulness. A separate study found the three triarchic facets are represented distinctly in the checklist, with boldness through the interpersonal facet, and that boldness distinguishes psychopathy from the far more common antisocial personality disorder diagnosis.
strength.boundaries: Two boundaries that matter. The same analysis found unexpected sex differences, with boldness less relevant to psychopathy in women. And self-report measures of psychopathy raise an obvious problem the literature acknowledges: the construct includes deceitfulness, and the measurement asks people to report honestly about themselves.

body.def: Psychopathy has no single agreed measurement, and the choice of instrument changes what the construct is. The dominant clinical instrument is an interview-and-file-based checklist used in forensic settings; self-report measures have grown steadily more common in community samples.
body.mech: The triarchic model decomposes psychopathy into three facets: boldness (social dominance, stress resilience, calm under threat), meanness, and disinhibition. The clinical checklist covers disinhibition and meanness substantially and directly, but captures boldness only indirectly and modestly — and because it relies on antisocially deviant indicators, it is ill-suited to studying psychopathy outside criminal populations.
body.app: Popular writing about 'psychopaths in the boardroom' usually rests on self-report community measures that include boldness, which is precisely the component under dispute. Findings from forensic checklist studies do not transfer to that population automatically.

sources: Patrick, Fowles & Krueger (2009) — the triarchic model
Hare (2003), PCL-R
Lilienfeld & Andrews (1996) — Psychopathic Personality Inventory
Venables, Hall & Patrick (2013), Psychological Medicine — triarchic facets in the PCL-R and ASPD
Are fearless dominance traits superfluous in operationalizing psychopathy? (2016), N=1,565 adult offenders
Evans & Tully (2016), Aggression and Violent Behavior 27 — review of the Triarchic Psychopathy Measure
open: Whether boldness is a component of psychopathy or an adaptive trait that happens to co-occur with it. This is the field's central unresolved question and it determines whether 'successful psychopath' is a coherent category.

label: What dark traits actually predict

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: The counterproductive-behaviour link is the robust part. The job-performance link is weaker and does not survive multivariate analysis, which matters: the folk claim is that dark traits help you get ahead, and the evidence is that they mainly predict harm done rather than success achieved.
strength.magnitude: A meta-analysis drawing on 245 independent samples (N=43,907) from reports published between 1951 and 2011 found that reductions in job performance quality were consistently associated with increases in Machiavellianism and psychopathy, and that counterproductive work behaviour increased with all three traits. Multivariate analysis showed the dark triad explains moderate amounts of variance in counterproductivity but not in job performance. A later update with over 50% more data found narcissism remained the largest unique predictor of counterproductive work behaviour after controlling for the Big Five.
strength.boundaries: The associations were moderated by contextual factors including authority and culture. Notably, the update found that the original meta-analysis's inference of cross-cultural moderation hinged on a single dataset from Bangladesh — a good example of how a moderator claim can rest on far less than it appears to.

body.def: The empirical question underneath the popular fascination: do these traits help or hurt the people who have them, and at what?
body.mech: The dominant framing treats dark traits as exploitative strategies that extract short-term gains at the cost of relationships — a social-exchange account.
