body.inter: The three traits were positively related to one another but, in this analysis, sufficiently distinctive to warrant separate treatment — which sits in tension with the near-total latent overlap found elsewhere.
body.app: 'Dark traits succeed short-term and fail long-term' is a satisfying story and the evidence for the first half is thinner than for the second. What replicates is that they predict counterproductive behaviour; what does not clearly replicate is that they produce performance advantages at any horizon.

sources: O'Boyle, Forsyth, Banks & McDaniel (2012), Journal of Applied Psychology 97(3):557–579 — 245 samples, N=43,907
Grijalva & Newman (2015) — narcissism and CWB meta-analysis update, k=16, N=4,424
open: Whether any dark-trait advantage exists at all once measurement overlap with Honesty-Humility and publication bias are both accounted for.

label: Early deprivation — the natural experiment

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: A randomised controlled trial run independently in Bucharest reached convergent conclusions, which is unusually strong for developmental research. Substantial heterogeneity in trajectories means group findings do not describe individuals.
strength.magnitude: The duration threshold is the headline. By age 6, children with under six months of deprivation were largely indistinguishable from non-deprived UK adoptees. For many — but not all — of those with more than six months, significant impairment of social and cognitive functioning persisted through adolescence and into young adulthood.
strength.boundaries: Two boundaries cut in opposite directions and both matter. Cognitive impairment showed adult remission — the deficit was not permanent. But the authors' own summary is blunt: extended early deprivation was associated with long-term deleterious effects on wellbeing that appeared insusceptible to years of nurturance and support in adoptive families. Good later environments did not undo everything.

body.def: The closest thing to a controlled experiment on early experience that ethics permits. Children who spent from birth up to 43 months in severely depriving Romanian institutions were adopted into socioeconomically advantaged, stable, caring UK families, and followed to adulthood.
body.mech: Because adoption allocated children to radically better environments at differing ages, duration of deprivation can be separated from what came after — and because the adoptive families were uniformly good, later environment is held roughly constant.
body.app: Both the strong-determinism story and the blank-slate recovery story are wrong. Duration mattered, recovery was real and partial, and which outcome you look at changes the answer.

sources: Sonuga-Barke, Kennedy, Kumsta, Knights, Golm, Rutter, Maughan, Schlotz & Kreppner (2017), The Lancet 389(10078):1539–1548
Rutter, Kumsta, Schlotz & Sonuga-Barke (2012), Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry — the natural-experiment design
Rutter et al. (1999), Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry — quasi-autistic patterns
Rodriguez-Perez, Kennedy, Barker, Kreppner, Solerdelcoll & Sonuga-Barke (2023), JCPP 64(9):1292–1302
open: Why some children with extended deprivation showed no lasting deprivation-specific problems. The heterogeneity is large and largely unexplained.

label: Randomised foster care (Bucharest)

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Convergent with the non-randomised Romanian adoptee cohort, and followed across nearly 20 years of assessments with a comprehensive multilevel synthesis.
strength.magnitude: Average age at foster placement was 22 months (range 6–31). Cognitive outcomes for children remaining in institutions were markedly below both the fostered and never-institutionalised groups, and gains were most marked for the youngest children placed. Benefit persisted at ages 8 and 12, and at the 18-year follow-up — sixteen years after randomisation — those assigned to foster care had IQ scores 9 points higher, about 0.6 standard deviations. Mediation analysis indicated the effect ran partly through higher-quality caregiving and attachment security.
strength.boundaries: Placement after 24 months was associated with lower expressive language, which is the trial's timing evidence. High-quality foster care was purpose-built for the study; ordinary foster care is not necessarily equivalent.

body.def: A randomised controlled trial of foster care as an alternative to institutional care — the only experiment of its kind. 136 institutionalised children were randomly assigned to high-quality foster care or continued institutional care, with a never-institutionalised community comparison group.
body.mech: Random assignment removes the usual confound that children who leave institutions may differ from those who stay. The causal claim here is genuinely causal.
body.app: A 0.6 SD causal effect on adult IQ from a caregiving intervention is one of the largest environmental effects in this atlas, and it sits in the same domain where twin studies report heritability near .80. Both are true.

sources: Nelson, Zeanah, Fox, Marshall, Smyke & Guthrie (2007), Science 318:1937–1940
Fox, Almas, Degnan, Nelson & Zeanah (2011), JCPP 52:919–928
Almas, Degnan, Nelson, Zeanah & Fox (2016), Developmental Psychology 52(11):1858–1866
Foster care leads to sustained cognitive gains following severe early deprivation (2022), PNAS — age-18 follow-up, N=135
Zeanah, Fox & Nelson — comprehensive multilevel analysis, American Journal of Psychiatry
open: Whether the effect generalises from extreme deprivation to ordinary variation in caregiving quality. Nothing here licenses that inference.

label: Sensitive periods

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: Two independent designs, one observational and one randomised, converged on timing effects. That is the strength of the claim. What remains weak is any mechanism specifying why those particular ages.
strength.magnitude: Two timing thresholds emerged independently. In the Romanian adoptee cohort, under six months of deprivation produced outcomes largely indistinguishable from non-deprived adoptees while longer exposure did not. In the randomised trial, placement after 24 months was associated with lower expressive language, and cognitive gains were most marked for the youngest children placed.
strength.boundaries: These are thresholds for recovery from severe deprivation, not general windows for ordinary learning. The popular version — that the first three years determine everything — does not follow, and the same studies show adult remission of cognitive impairment, which a strict critical period would not permit.

body.def: The proposal that there are developmental windows during which experience has outsized and hard-to-reverse effects — weaker than 'critical periods', which imply an absolute cutoff.
body.mech: If a window exists, outcomes should depend on the timing of an experience and not only its presence or duration.
body.app: Used to justify enormous claims about early-years parenting. The evidence is about recovery from severe deprivation, and does not establish that ordinary variation in early enrichment has comparable timing sensitivity.

sources: Sonuga-Barke et al. (2017), The Lancet 389(10078):1539–1548
Windsor, Moraru, Nelson, Fox & Zeanah — language outcomes and the 24-month threshold
Nelson, Zeanah, Fox et al. (2007), Science 318:1937–1940
open: Whether any sensitive period has been demonstrated for social or emotional development outside conditions of severe deprivation.

label: Adolescent risk-taking

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: Its own proponents concede the model is insufficiently nuanced while defending it as a useful heuristic. A refinement proposes that only a subgroup with pre-existing self-regulation deficits shows the imbalance and the attendant maladaptive risk-taking — which is a substantially narrower claim than the popular one.
strength.magnitude: The developmental trajectories it predicts do hold: sensation-seeking follows an inverted U and self-regulation increases monotonically, observed across cultures.
strength.boundaries: The imbalance hypothesis itself is much weaker than the trajectories. Critics note a lack of specificity and questionable falsifiability — it is unclear how one would show strong evidence that the imbalance is not implicated — leading to the argument that dual systems models are informative heuristics rather than testable theories. Empirical evidence of a mid-adolescent peak is not unequivocal: the peak age varies by behaviour and it is often late adolescents, not middle adolescents, who are most reckless. Many risk behaviours peak after adolescence, possibly for reasons of opportunity rather than neurodevelopment.

body.def: The dual systems model: risk-taking peaks in mid-adolescence because a reward-sensitive socioemotional system matures faster than the cognitive control system, producing a temporary imbalance.
body.mech: Heightened reward reactivity against a backdrop of still-maturing control. As control catches up, risk-taking falls.
body.app: This model underwrites a great deal of policy and parenting advice about the teenage brain. The trajectory findings support the general picture; the specific imbalance mechanism is contested and may not be testable as stated.

sources: Steinberg (2010) and Somerville, Jones & Casey (2010) — the model
Pfeifer & Allen (2012; 2016), Trends in Cognitive Sciences — critique
Willoughby, Good, Adachi, Hamza & Tavernier (2013) — peak-age evidence
Defoe, Dubas, Figner & van Aken (2014) — meta-analysis
Meisel et al. (2019), Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience — statistical evaluation of the imbalance hypothesis
Romer, Reyna & Satterthwaite — the subgroup refinement
open: Whether the imbalance hypothesis can be operationalised in a way that permits disconfirmation. Several reviewers argue it currently cannot.

label: General intelligence (g)

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The manifold replicates about as robustly as anything in this atlas. The causal interpretation does not have comparable support, because a factor extracted from correlations does not identify its own cause.
strength.magnitude: The positive manifold is described in its own literature as among the most replicated findings in psychology: it does not depend on the nature of the task and appears across varied populations. The extracted general factor accounts for roughly 40–50% of variance across cognitive tasks. Heritability rises across the lifespan, reaching 60–80% in adults.
strength.boundaries: The critical distinction, and the one almost every popular treatment collapses: the statistical phenomenon is real and none of g's critics dispute it. The dispute is what it represents. The mutualism model reproduces the hierarchical factor structure, the low predictability from early childhood performance, the rising heritability of g and the Jensen effect — all without positing a single capacity.

body.def: Scores on cognitive tasks correlate positively with each other — the 'positive manifold'. Spearman proposed in 1904 that a single general factor underlies this. The manifold is settled; what it means is not.
body.mech: Factor analysis extracts a general factor from any diverse cognitive battery. The dominant interpretation is a single underlying capacity. The leading alternative — mutualism — shows the positive manifold can emerge purely from beneficial interactions between cognitive processes during development, with no single underlying g factor playing any role.
body.intra: A general factor being real as a statistical regularity does not mean you possess a quantity of it. The same data are consistent with abilities that grew together through mutual reinforcement.
body.app: Predictive validity for academic achievement, job performance and health outcomes is genuinely high — but see the overcorrection node, because the headline validity figures in personnel selection were revised sharply downward in 2022.

sources: Spearman (1904) — the original proposal
van der Maas, Dolan, Grasman, Wicherts, Huizenga & Raijmakers (2006), Psychological Review 113(4):842–861 — mutualism model of the positive manifold
Jensen (1998), The g Factor
Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens (2022), Journal of Applied Psychology
open: Whether g is a causal entity or an emergent statistical property of developmentally interacting abilities. Twenty years after the mutualism model this remains unresolved, and the two are not distinguishable by factor analysis alone.

label: Brain training and far transfer

strength.label: failed
strength.replication: Four comprehensive meta-analyses converge: training improves the trained task and, less so, similar tasks, with little or no effect on unrelated cognitive tests — especially when compared against active controls that rule out placebo effects. A re-analysis of the most favourable n-back dataset found the overall effect size falls to around zero when experimental groups are compared to active controls rather than passive ones. The choice of control group is what separates the positive literature from the negative one.
strength.magnitude: A meta-analysis of 87 publications with 145 experimental comparisons, restricted to pretest-posttest designs with control groups, found reliable improvements immediately after training on intermediate transfer — verbal and visuospatial working memory. For far transfer — nonverbal ability, verbal ability, word decoding, reading comprehension, arithmetic — there was no convincing evidence of any reliable improvement when compared against a treated control condition.
strength.boundaries: Near transfer is real. You do get better at the trained task, and somewhat better at tasks resembling it. That is not what the products claim.

body.def: The claim that training working memory — n-back tasks and similar — produces general cognitive benefits, raising intelligence and improving unrelated skills. A commercial industry rests on it.
body.mech: The rationale was that working memory and fluid intelligence correlate strongly, probably through shared reliance on executive attention, so training one should raise the other.
body.intra: Training a cognitive task makes you better at that task. There is no established route from that to being generally smarter.
body.app: This is the clearest case in the atlas of a commercial sector built on an effect that does not survive an active control condition.

sources: Melby-Lervåg, Redick & Hulme (2016), Perspectives on Psychological Science 11(4):512–534
Melby-Lervåg & Hulme (2013; 2016) — original and re-analysis
Au et al. (2015) and the subsequent active-control re-analyses
Schwaighofer, Fischer & Bühner (2015); Weicker, Villringer & Thöne-Otto (2016)
open: Whether any cognitive training regimen produces far transfer in any population. Some meta-analyses report effects in specific age or patient groups, and those claims have not been separately audited here.

label: Deliberate practice

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: Actively disputed. The original theory's proponents contest the coding of studies and the treatment of measurement error; a separate meta-analysis of music found a much higher corrected correlation. A published correction to the meta-analysis itself adjusted several models. The meta-analysts' reply concedes none of the criticisms overturn their central conclusion — that deliberate practice matters less than claimed. Both sides agree practice is important; they disagree about whether it is dominant.
strength.magnitude: A meta-analysis covering all major domains where deliberate practice has been studied found it explained 26% of the variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education, and less than 1% in professions. Restricting to reliable variance raises these — 41% for games, 33% for music, 28% for sports, 7% for education — but the overall figure is about 19% of reliable variance, leaving roughly 81% potentially explainable by other factors.
strength.boundaries: The domain gradient is the finding people skip. Practice explains a quarter of the variance in chess and almost none in professional work. Whatever governs how good a professional becomes, it is largely not hours logged.

body.def: The proposal that individual differences in expert performance largely reflect differences in accumulated deliberate practice — structured activity designed specifically to improve performance. The source of the popular '10,000 hours' idea.
body.mech: If practice is the dominant cause, its correlation with performance should be very high and other factors should matter little.
body.intra: Practice is necessary and reliably insufficient. The honest expectation is that structured effort explains a meaningful minority of where you end up, not most of it.
body.app: '10,000 hours' was a popularisation that the underlying research does not support as a general law. The meta-analytic answer is domain-dependent and, outside games and music, small.

sources: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014), Psychological Science 25(8):1608–1618
Corrigendum (2018), Psychological Science 29(7):1202–1204
Macnamara, Moreau & Hambrick (2016) — sports-specific meta-analysis
Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet & Campitelli (2014), Intelligence 45:34–45
Platz et al. — the music counter-analysis, and Hambrick et al.'s published reply
open: What accounts for the remaining ~80% of reliable variance. Neither camp has a satisfying answer, and 'talent' is a label for the gap rather than an explanation of it.

label: The Flynn effect and its reversal

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: Three studies from overlapping research groups, two supporting the differentiation account and one not. This is emerging work on a real phenomenon, not an established explanation, which is why it is graded moderate rather than solid.
strength.magnitude: A cohort-comparison study of two population-representative German-speaking samples (N=1,267) across six measurement-invariant subscales from 2005 to 2024 found substantial declines in single-factor g assessments (ΔR² −.037 to −.066) alongside meaningful score increases in every domain (d from 0.18 to 1.24), with the largest gains in the lower tail of the distribution.
strength.boundaries: Not settled. An earlier Austrian study (N=1,392, 2005–2018) found the same directional trend in positive manifold strength but the change was not statistically significant, and a 2025 study of Austrian armed-forces data found substantial Flynn effects in most subscales with no evidence of any meaningful change in positive manifold strength.

body.def: Generational gains in IQ test scores, typically reported as 2–4 points per decade across the twentieth century. In recent decades the pattern has become inconsistent, with stagnation and reversals in several countries.
body.mech: A newly proposed explanation: the inconsistency may be driven by a weakening of the positive manifold itself, as abilities differentiate and specialise in the general population — so scores rise in individual domains while the general factor binding them weakens.
body.app: Both 'we are getting smarter' and 'we are getting dumber' are being asserted from this literature. What the data show is domain-specific gains alongside a possibly weakening general factor — which is neither.

sources: Pietschnig et al. (2024), Intelligence 107:101867 — N=1,267, 2005–2024
Increasing IQ Test Scores and Decreasing g (2024), Journal of Intelligence 12(12):130 — N=1,392, non-significant
Generational IQ test score changes and the positive manifold (2025), Frontiers in Psychology 16:1547520 — no manifold change found
open: Whether the positive manifold is genuinely weakening. Three studies, two directions, same broad research community.

label: Fundamental social motives

body.def: An evolutionary account of recurring adaptive problems humans evolved dedicated motive systems for: self-protection, disease avoidance, affiliation, status, mate acquisition, mate retention, kin care. Renovates Maslow's pyramid.
body.mech: An active motive redirects attention, memory and social inference toward that goal. Warmth-reading plausibly serves affiliation and self-protection; competence-reading serves status and mate quality.
body.app: A buyer under a self-protection motive processes a pitch differently from one under a status motive.

sources: Kenrick, Griskevicius, Neuberg & Schaller (2010), Perspectives on Psychological Science
open: Downgraded from solid in Cycle 1. v1 quoted a specific country count and sample size for the cross-cultural validation that was not re-verified, so it has been removed rather than repeated. The framework is a functional-level hypothesis about evolved design; it is not established by the measurement traditions in this atlas and the evidence for discrete dedicated motive systems is weaker than v1 implied.

label: Need to belong

body.def: A fundamental drive to form and maintain a minimum number of lasting, positive relationships, with measurable consequences for health and cognition when unmet.
body.mech: Satisfied by frequent pleasant interaction inside a stable frame of mutual concern — both contact and perceived care are required.
body.app: Buyers protect their standing inside their own organisation; a deal that threatens it dies quietly.

sources: Baumeister & Leary (1995), Psychological Bulletin

label: Sociometer theory

body.def: Self-esteem functions as a gauge of relational value — how much others accept and value you — rather than a free-standing quantity.
body.mech: Perceived rejection lowers the gauge and triggers repair behaviour, which is why status and approval feel existential.
body.app: Removing blame risk moves stalled decisions; the fear is relational, not financial.

sources: Leary, Tambor, Terdal & Downs (1995), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

label: Big Five (OCEAN)

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The five-factor structure itself replicates widely. The applied validity figures are where the contest is: Kepes & McDaniel (2015) applied sensitivity analyses and argued conscientiousness validity is overestimated by publication bias. A separate problem for the biological reading of traits: a genome-wide analysis found detectable common-variant heritability only for neuroticism and openness, and none for extraversion, agreeableness or conscientiousness.
strength.magnitude: Conscientiousness is the most consistent job-performance predictor of the five, but the magnitude is contested and smaller than commonly quoted. Barrick & Mount reported a corrected mean validity of .22; Salgado .25 in European samples; one large synthesis ρ = .27; more recent work reports observed (uncorrected) validities around .13–.20 and a meta-analytic r̄ of .17 (k=102, n=23,305).
strength.boundaries: Predicts aggregate tendencies, not single acts — and the person–situation node explains why that is the strongest available claim. Validity estimates depend heavily on correction methods (see the Sackett correction node) and trait heritability estimates depend just as heavily on research design (see personality heritability). Cycle 4 adds the largest boundary: the five-factor structure has been recovered almost exclusively in literate, urban populations, and the first test in a largely illiterate indigenous society failed on every criterion attempted.

plain.what: Five dials that capture most of what differs between personalities: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and emotional volatility.
plain.why: It is the measuring stick every other personality system gets judged against, including the ones sold at work.
plain.catch: Dials, not boxes. Nobody is 'an extravert' — everyone sits somewhere on all five at once.

body.def: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — five continuous trait dimensions recovered from factor analysis of trait language across languages. The reference standard other personality models are judged against.
body.mech: Traits are dimensions, not types. Extraversion and Agreeableness are the interpersonal traits and map onto the two social-evaluation axes.
body.intra: You are a point in five continuous dimensions, not a letter code.
body.app: Conscientiousness is the defensible trait to weigh in selection — but at ~.17–.27, not as a dominant predictor. v1's '.20–.30' presented the top of a contested range as settled.

sources: Barrick & Mount (1991) — corrected mean validity .22
Salgado (1997) — European samples, corrected .25
Kepes & McDaniel (2015), PLoS ONE — publication-bias sensitivity analysis
Goldberg (1990; 1993), American Psychologist
open: Facet-level structure, cross-cultural invariance of all five, and whether trait change interventions do anything durable. Queued for the personality cycle.

label: DISC / colour model

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: The honest position is 'under-tested independently', not 'debunked'. Most validation evidence is vendor-produced. That is a weaker claim than v1 made and a fairer one.
strength.magnitude: Internal consistency is reported around .70–.85 and test-retest is acceptable. Independent, peer-reviewed confirmatory factor analysis of the four-factor structure is thin, and published criterion-related validity linking DISC scores to job performance is minimal. Notably, the publisher's own historical account states that factor analysis of the precursor instrument produced two factors, not four.
strength.boundaries: Adequate as a shared vocabulary for adapting communication style. Not defensible for hiring, promotion, or predicting performance.

body.def: Four behavioural styles — Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, Conscientiousness (Erikson's Red, Yellow, Green, Blue) — descended from Marston's 1928 theory of emotions, operationalised by Walter Clarke from the 1940s.
body.mech: A four-quadrant scheme sitting on axes closely resembling dominance and affiliation. Its intuitive appeal comes from being a coarse crop of a space that other frameworks recover more rigorously.
body.intra: Translate rather than adopt: Red ≈ high agency; Green ≈ high communion; Yellow ≈ high on both; Blue ≈ conscientious and reserved.
body.inter: Useful for naming a communication mismatch out loud. Stops being useful the moment it becomes a label a person is expected to live inside.
body.app: Used for team training and sales-style adaptation. Misused for selection, where the absence of criterion validity means it is decoration with a price tag.

sources: Marston (1928), Emotions of Normal People
Everything DiSC / Wiley published history — factor analyses of the precursor produced two factors approximating Marston's axes
open: Whether any independent peer-reviewed CFA of the four-factor structure exists. v1 cited one that does not. Queued.

label: Interpersonal circumplex

body.def: A circular model of interpersonal behaviour on two orthogonal axes — dominance↔submission and warmth↔hostility — with traits at angles around the circle. Developed in clinical psychology decades before the social-cognition Big Two.
body.mech: Complementarity: warmth invites warmth, hostility invites hostility, dominance invites submission. It predicts what your behaviour elicits, not only what you are like.
body.app: Your opening register sets the other person's. If people go quiet around you, check whether you are pulling submission.

sources: Leary (1957), Interpersonal Diagnosis of Personality
Wiggins (1979), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
open: Whether circumplex orthogonality survives the curvilinearity finding. Unresolved and worth a cycle.

label: Self-Determination Theory

body.def: Three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence, relatedness. Satisfying all three predicts intrinsic motivation and wellbeing; controlling conditions undermine it.
body.mech: Competence and relatedness correspond to the two social-evaluation axes. Autonomy is the third need that no influence framework in the applied tier names, and it is what separates influence that lands as care from influence that lands as control.
body.app: A testable target for any relationship: does being around you raise the other person's competence, connection and self-direction.

sources: Ryan & Deci (2000), American Psychologist
Ryan & Deci (2017), Self-Determination Theory, Guilford
open: Effect sizes and cross-cultural universality of the three needs were not verified this cycle.

label: Need for cognitive closure

body.def: A motivated desire for a firm answer and aversion to ambiguity — both a stable trait and a state raised by time pressure, fatigue and noise.
body.mech: Two components: urgency (seize an answer) and permanence (freeze on it). High closure need produces faster judgements and heavier stereotyping.
body.app: A tired, rushed decision-maker seizes the first coherent answer. The application of this construct to push-pull seduction tactics is my inference, not a seduction study. [synthesis]

sources: Webster & Kruglanski (1994), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Kruglanski & Webster (1996), Psychological Review

label: Dual-process cognition

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: They report a consensus emerging among both critics and leading proponents that the classic Type 1 / Type 2 distinction is flawed. The paper drew immediate published replies arguing they overstate it — that one need not assert alignment among all features to defend a dichotomy on one specific feature. So this is a live dispute, not a settled debunking. But v1 and v2 graded this node solid and described the framework as established architecture, which is not defensible.
strength.magnitude: Enormously influential beyond psychology: the World Bank and the Institute of Medicine issued 2015 reports endorsing the Type 1 / Type 2 distinction and urging decision-makers and medical practitioners to rely on Type 2 thinking.
strength.boundaries: Re-audited in Cycle 2 and downgraded from solid. Melnikoff & Bargh argue the two-types framework lacks empirical support, contradicts established findings and is internally incoherent: very few processes fit cleanly into either category and most possess a mixture of features. Processing can be unconscious but intentional, or fast but conscious. Their structural charge is sharper still — that the typology resists disconfirmation, because a failed prediction can always be attributed to contamination between systems or an unspecified third factor.

body.def: The claim that cognition divides into two types: one unintentional, uncontrollable, unconscious and efficient; the other intentional, controllable, conscious and inefficient. Popularised as System 1 and System 2.
body.mech: The framework's power comes from the assumption that these four features cluster — that fast also means unconscious, automatic and uncontrollable. That assumption is the part under attack.
body.intra: 'Slow down and think' is not a complete intervention, because fast is not reliably the same as wrong and slow is not reliably the same as deliberate.
body.app: This node is a hub — heuristics, biases, persuasion routes and automaticity all link through it, so the downgrade propagates. Anything here leaning on a clean fast/slow partition inherits the uncertainty. The earlier phrasing, that most judgements run on System 1 with System 2 rationalising afterwards, has been removed as an assertion the evidence does not support.

sources: Melnikoff & Bargh (2018), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 22(4):280–293 — 'The Mythical Number Two'
Evans & Stanovich (2013), Perspectives on Psychological Science — the defended version
Keren & Schul (2009), Perspectives on Psychological Science — earlier critical evaluation
Osman (2018) and Chater (2018), Trends in Cognitive Sciences — published replies
Tversky & Kahneman (1974), Science
open: Whether any single feature — autonomy, for instance — can carry a defensible dichotomy once the feature cluster is abandoned. That is what the defenders propose and it is unresolved.

label: Loss aversion

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: A live, published dispute rather than a replication failure. Gal & Rucker (2018) in Journal of Consumer Psychology, published alongside commentaries; Simonson & Kivetz replied that the conclusion was overstated while conceding the message has value; Mrkva, Johnson, Gächter & Herrmann replied under the title 'loss aversion has moderators, but reports of its death are greatly exaggerated'.
strength.magnitude: The 2:1 ratio comes from the original formulation and should be treated as an upper bound rather than a constant. Gal & Rucker argue the evidence supports a conditional rather than general claim, and that endowment and default effects can be explained without asymmetric weighting — for example by simple inertia.
strength.boundaries: Weak or absent at small stakes on several tests. Effects attributed to it may reflect risk aversion or a preference for inaction.

body.def: The claim that losses loom larger than equivalent gains — classically around 2:1 — with risk-aversion for gains and risk-seeking to avoid losses, judged against a reference point.
body.mech: Reference-dependence in prospect theory. Invoked to explain status-quo bias, the endowment effect and why framing the cost of inaction can outperform framing the gain.
body.intra: Sunk cost reasoning is the everyday form. Whether it is loss aversion or plain inertia is exactly what is in dispute.
body.app: Loss framing is a real tool but not a law. v1 cited the critique without the defence and so implied the concept was quietly deflating; it is contested in both directions.

sources: Kahneman & Tversky (1979), Econometrica
Gal & Rucker (2018), Journal of Consumer Psychology 28(3):497–516
Simonson & Kivetz (2018), Journal of Consumer Psychology — commentary
Mrkva, Johnson, Gächter & Herrmann (2020), Journal of Consumer Psychology — reply
open: Whether a general asymmetry exists at all, or only context-specific ones. Currently unresolved in the literature.

label: Anchoring

body.def: The first number or reference point disproportionately shapes subsequent estimates, even when arbitrary, and even when people know it is happening.
body.mech: Insufficient adjustment away from the starting point.
body.app: Control the first number in a negotiation, or re-anchor explicitly before proceeding.

sources: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), Science
Furnham & Boo (2011), Journal of Socio-Economics — review

label: Availability heuristic

body.def: Judging frequency or likelihood by how readily examples come to mind, so vivid and recent instances crowd out base rates.
body.mech: Ease of recall is mistaken for probability.
body.app: One vivid loss distorts your read of the next situation more than your actual hit rate should allow.

sources: Tversky & Kahneman (1973), Cognitive Psychology

label: Cognitive dissonance

body.def: Holding inconsistent beliefs, or acting against a belief, produces discomfort that motivates attitude change to restore consistency.
body.mech: Effort justification and insufficient justification. Underpins commitment and consistency effects.
body.app: Effort spent on something increases how much you value it, in both directions.

sources: Festinger (1957), A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance
Festinger & Carlsmith (1959), Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

label: Self-perception theory

body.def: People infer their own attitudes by observing their own behaviour, especially when internal cues are weak — the rival account of dissonance findings.
body.mech: Act first, infer the attitude afterwards. No internal discomfort is required for the effect.
body.app: Getting someone to articulate a position in their own words shifts them toward it.

sources: Bem (1972), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology

label: Fundamental attribution error

body.def: Explaining others' behaviour by character while under-weighting situation, and doing the reverse for oneself.
body.mech: Strongest under cognitive load; weaker in East Asian samples, which makes it partly cultural rather than fundamental.
body.app: A quiet counterpart is usually situationally constrained, not uninterested.

sources: Ross (1977), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology
Gilbert & Malone (1995), Psychological Bulletin
open: Cross-cultural moderation makes the name a misnomer. Queued for the culture cycle.

label: Dunning–Kruger effect

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: Actively disputed rather than settled. Hiller (2023) argued the null resulted from a scale-transformation choice; Gignac replied that re-analysis using Hiller's recommended transformation still found no effect; Dunkel, Nedelec & van der Linden (2023) published a response and replication.
strength.magnitude: Gignac & Zajenkowski (2020), N=929 community participants using self-assessed intelligence and Advanced Raven's Progressive Matrices, found no statistically significant heteroscedasticity and an essentially linear relation between measured and self-assessed intelligence — both contrary to the hypothesis. Gignac (2024) modelled the effect as negligible and confined to a limited segment of the population.
strength.boundaries: Applies to self-assessment of cognitive ability. Claims about other skills are extrapolation.

plain.what: The idea that the less skilled you are, the more you overestimate yourself.
plain.why: It is one of the most repeated claims on the internet and the statistics behind it are disputed.
plain.catch: Critics show the famous chart can be produced from data containing no such effect at all, which makes it possibly a measurement artefact.

body.def: The hypothesis that people with less of an ability are worse at estimating that ability, so low performers overestimate themselves most.
body.mech: The original test plotted self-assessed against objective scores across quartiles. Critics argue that method confounds regression to the mean with a general better-than-average effect, and can generate the classic figure from data containing no Dunning–Kruger effect at all.
body.intra: Calibrate against feedback and track record, not introspection.
body.inter: Do not use it as a label for other people. The label outran the evidence by a wide margin.
body.app: Widely deployed in management training as 'the incompetent are the most confident'. That version is not supported.

sources: Kruger & Dunning (1999), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Gignac & Zajenkowski (2020), Intelligence 80, 'The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact'
Hiller (2023), Intelligence 97 — comment
Dunkel, Nedelec & van der Linden (2023), Intelligence 96 — response and replication
Gignac (2024), Intelligence 104
open: Whether a small genuine effect exists in a narrow low-ability band. Gignac's 2024 modelling suggests possibly yes, but negligible.

label: Halo effect

plain.what: One good thing about someone bleeds into everything else you judge about them.
plain.why: It is why attractive or confident people get credited with unrelated qualities they may not have.
plain.catch: Knowing about it does not switch it off. It happens while the overall impression is forming.

body.def: A single salient positive attribute colours judgements of unrelated attributes.
body.mech: Perceivers cannot fully separate attributes when forming an overall impression.
body.app: One accurate early technical detail casts a competence impression over the rest of a meeting.

sources: Thorndike (1920), Journal of Applied Psychology
Nisbett & Wilson (1977), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

label: Thin slices & rapid judgements

plain.what: People form judgements about you in seconds, sometimes from about a tenth of a second of your face.
plain.why: The judgement is largely made before you have said anything much.
plain.catch: Fast judgements beat chance but are not accurate. More time raises confidence more than it raises accuracy.

body.def: Very brief observations — seconds of behaviour, or around 100 ms of a face — produce trait judgements that predict some outcomes above chance. Longer exposure raises confidence more than accuracy.
body.mech: Trustworthiness and competence are judged first and automatically.
body.app: You are placed before you speak. That licenses managing first impressions; it does not license trusting your own snap read of someone's intent.

sources: Ambady & Rosenthal (1992), Psychological Bulletin
Willis & Todorov (2006), Psychological Science
Todorov et al. (2015), Annual Review of Psychology
open: Accuracy versus consensus is the crux: agreement between perceivers is high, accuracy is much weaker. Not re-verified this cycle.

label: Mere exposure

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: Two independent meta-analyses (Bornstein 1989; Montoya et al. 2017) support a robust effect within those boundaries. The 2017 paper concludes that existing theoretical models do not adequately explain the pattern.
strength.magnitude: Montoya, Horton, Vevea, Citkowicz & Lauber (2017) estimated parameters from 268 curve estimates across 81 articles and found a positive slope with a negative quadratic term — the inverted U. Effect sizes were larger for ideographs, nonsense words and abstract images than for photographs.
strength.boundaries: The single most important boundary, and one v1 omitted entirely: the inverted-U pattern held for visual stimuli but the meta-analysis found no evidence of the effect for auditory stimuli. It also held for exposures shorter than 10 seconds and longer than a minute, and for ratings taken after all stimuli were presented.

body.def: Repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking, including without conscious recognition, following an inverted-U rather than a straight line.
body.mech: Familiarity produces processing fluency, which is experienced as mild positive affect and misattributed to the stimulus.
body.intra: You like what you have seen before. Audit whether a preference is preference or familiarity.
body.inter: Repeated low-stakes contact does more work than infrequent high-effort gestures.
body.app: Supports consistent contact cadence over one large push — but past the peak, more contact reduces liking. v1 asserted the peak sits at 10–20 exposures. That number is not in the source and has been removed; the meta-analysis models the curve's shape, not a universal turning point.

sources: Zajonc (1968), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Montoya, Horton, Vevea, Citkowicz & Lauber (2017), Psychological Bulletin 143(5):459–498
Bornstein (1989), Psychological Bulletin — earlier meta-analysis
open: Why the effect fails for auditory stimuli, and where the turning point actually sits for faces and people rather than ideographs.

label: Similarity–attraction

body.def: Perceived similarity predicts initial attraction; actual similarity matters less, and the effect weakens in established relationships.
body.mech: Perceived similarity provides consensual validation of one's own views.
body.app: Real common ground found early helps; manufactured similarity is detected.

sources: Byrne (1971), The Attraction Paradigm
Montoya, Horton & Kirchner (2008), Journal of Social and Personal Relationships — meta-analysis

label: Chameleon effect (mimicry)

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: Re-audited in Cycle 2. The original paper was verified (JPSP 76(6):893–910) and the 2024 field study is a genuine, published downgrade signal from the authors' own Bayesian analysis. I could not verify a secondary claim, repeated in several non-academic sources, that a 2020 meta-analysis specifically downgraded the mimicry-causes-liking link. That claim is not in this node and sits in the unverified queue, because a blog asserting a meta-analysis exists is not a meta-analysis.
strength.magnitude: The original paper is one of the most-cited findings in modern social psychology. Experiment 1 showed unintentional motor matching between strangers; Experiment 2 had confederates mimic participants and found increased liking and smoother interaction. A 2024 pair of field experiments (total N=460) found mimicry increased the likelihood of donating to charity — including when a different person made the request — but not the amount donated, and the authors' Bayesian analyses indicate the effect is less strongly pronounced than previous research and theories assumed.
strength.boundaries: The effect is moderated. One study found the mimicry–liking link held for participants with prosocial value orientations but not for proself-oriented ones, so it is not universal. And the original sits inside the wider social-priming research programme, which became a central case of the replication crisis — guilt by association is not evidence, but it is a reason for caution about the surrounding literature.

body.def: People unconsciously adopt the postures, gestures and mannerisms of interaction partners, and being mimicked increases liking and the felt smoothness of the interaction.
body.mech: Proposed mechanism is the perception–behaviour link: merely perceiving another's behaviour raises the likelihood of performing it yourself.
body.inter: Natural mimicry is a sign rapport already exists rather than a tool that creates it. Deliberate mimicry is detectable and its downside when detected is not well studied.
body.app: Sales and negotiation training treats mirroring as a reliable lever. The honest position: a real effect, smaller than assumed, moderated by the other person's disposition, and inside a literature that has taken heavy replication damage.

sources: Chartrand & Bargh (1999), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 76(6):893–910
Muniak, Genschow, Dolinski, Grzyb & Kulesza (2024), Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 113:104620 — two field experiments, N=460
Stel, Rispens, Leliveld & Lokhorst (2011), European Journal of Social Psychology 41(3):269–274 — social value orientation moderates the mimicry–liking link
open: Whether a direct meta-analysis of mimicry on liking exists and what it found. Also: the cost of detected deliberate mimicry, which the applied literature never addresses.

label: Reciprocal self-disclosure

body.def: Disclosure produces liking and invites reciprocal disclosure; escalating mutual personal disclosure generates closeness quickly.
body.mech: Disclosure signals trust, the reciprocity norm returns it, and graduated depth prevents exposure.
body.app: Closeness is built by graduated mutual disclosure, not by one person interviewing the other.

sources: Collins & Miller (1994), Psychological Bulletin — meta-analysis
Aron, Melinat, Aron, Vallone & Bator (1997), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

label: Follow-up questions & likability

body.def: People who ask more questions, especially follow-ups on what was just said, are rated more likable by their actual conversation partners.
body.mech: Follow-ups signal responsiveness and elicit disclosure. The effect is specific to follow-ups rather than question count alone.
body.app: React to the last sentence rather than introducing a new topic.

sources: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

label: The '93% nonverbal' myth

plain.what: The famous claim that words are only 7% of communication is a misreading of two narrow experiments.
plain.why: It is quoted in almost every presentation-skills course and it does not mean what they say it means.
plain.catch: The real finding is small and specific: when your words and your tone disagree about how you feel about someone, people believe the tone.

body.def: The claim that words carry only 7% of communication misapplies two narrow 1967 experiments on single words spoken in mismatched tones, judging how much a speaker liked the listener.
body.mech: What survives: when words and tone contradict each other about feelings toward someone, the nonverbal channel usually wins. That is a narrow and real finding.
body.app: Any trainer citing 93% has not read the study. Congruence matters; the percentage does not exist.

sources: Mehrabian & Ferris (1967), Journal of Consulting Psychology
Mehrabian & Wiener (1967), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

label: Affect labeling

body.def: Putting a feeling into words reduces amygdala response and subjective distress.
body.mech: Implicit emotion regulation. Works on the person labelling, and accurate labelling of someone else's state appears to lower their defensiveness in real time.
body.app: Name the frustration under an objection before answering it. This is the mechanism the Voss techniques borrow.

sources: Lieberman et al. (2007), Psychological Science
Torre & Lieberman (2018), Emotion Review
open: How much of the interpersonal application follows from the intrapersonal neuroscience. Probably less than applied frameworks assume.

label: Motivational Interviewing & change talk

body.def: In MI, a person's own statements favouring change predict behaviour change, while the counsellor arguing for change elicits counter-argument.
body.mech: Reflective listening produces change talk; self-perception and dissonance then lock it in. Built on autonomy support rather than persuasion.
body.app: Reflect before responding. Arguing an objection makes it get defended harder.

sources: Miller & Rollnick (2023), Motivational Interviewing, 4th ed.
Moyers et al. (2009), Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
Magill et al. (2018), Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology — meta-analysis

label: Elaboration Likelihood Model

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: The dispute is decades old and unresolved. A 2022 head-to-head analysis concluded the unimodel does not rectify the ELM's conceptual limitations and does not explain anything the ELM cannot, so the challenger has not won either. But v1 and v2 graded this solid and stated the two routes as established fact, which the literature does not support.
strength.magnitude: One of the most influential frameworks in persuasion research since 1979, and the backbone of most applied persuasion training.
strength.boundaries: Re-audited in Cycle 3 and downgraded from solid, largely because the Cycle 2 dual-process downgrade applies here directly. Three substantive problems. First, Kruglanski's unimodel argues the two-route distinction is an artifact of how studies historically operationalised 'arguments' versus 'cues' rather than a real cognitive divide — that both are simply evidence bearing on a conclusion, with elaboration determining how carefully any information is processed rather than which kind gets processed. Second, a measurement problem: elaboration is rarely measured directly and is usually inferred from the manipulation, which makes the model hard to falsify. Third, much of the classic support comes from a narrow slice of persuasion — undergraduates, invented topics, single brief exposure — which differs sharply from sustained, socially embedded real persuasion.

body.def: Persuasion proceeds by a central route of argument evaluation when motivation and ability are high, or a peripheral route of cues when either is low. Central-route change is claimed to be more durable, more resistant to counter-argument and more predictive of behaviour.
body.mech: Motivation and ability jointly determine the route; missing either sends the person peripheral.
body.app: The practical advice survives the theoretical dispute reasonably well — motivated audiences with time engage with evidence, rushed ones respond to cues. What does not survive is treating central and peripheral as two distinct mechanisms rather than one process running at different depths.

sources: Petty & Cacioppo (1986), Communication and Persuasion
Kruglanski & Thompson (1999), Psychological Inquiry 10(2):83–109 — persuasion by a single route
Kruglanski, Chen, Pierro, Mannetti, Erb & Spiegel (2006) — persuasion according to the unimodel
El Hedhli & Zourrig (2022), Journal of Marketing Communications — ELM versus the unimodel
Kitchen, Kerr, Schultz, McColl & Pals (2014), European Journal of Marketing — review and critique
open: Whether elaboration can be measured independently of the manipulations used to induce it. Until it can, the model is hard to test properly.

label: Reciprocity

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: One study specifically tested whether the norm is internalised by having the original giver never learn of the return behaviour. Participants still returned the favour, and the tendency did not depend on whether the giver would find out — which rules out a purely reputational explanation. This is a re-audit that confirmed rather than downgraded, and reporting that matters as much as reporting the downgrades.
strength.magnitude: The classic demonstration had a confederate give participants an unrequested soft drink, then later ask them to buy raffle tickets; participants bought more after the favour. Re-audited in Cycle 5 and, unlike social proof, it held: subsequent investigations replicated the effect and supported the reciprocity-norm interpretation rather than a rival account.
strength.boundaries: Three moderators are well established in the literature: who the players are (whether the requester is the original giver, and whether the beneficiary is the person later asked), what the gift is (magnitude, and monetary versus non-monetary), and whether the request is larger in magnitude than the initial gift. The effect is not unconditional.

plain.what: Being given something makes you feel you owe something back.
plain.why: It is the best-evidenced of the classic influence tactics, and the one most often used on you.
plain.catch: It fires even when you did not ask for the gift. That is what makes it exploitable — an unsolicited favour removes your choice about who to owe.

body.def: Receiving something creates a felt obligation to return it. Formalised in 1960 as a norm that obligates people to respond to benefits with counter-benefits, argued to be a general requirement of stable social systems.
body.mech: The obligation can be triggered by an uninvited favour, which is what makes it exploitable — an unsolicited gift removes your ability to choose whom you become indebted to.
body.inter: Full attention functions as a gift, and the obligation it creates is real whether or not you intended it.
body.app: Free samples, no-obligation demonstrations and gifts inside fundraising letters are all this principle deployed deliberately. The honest use is to give real value first; the manipulative use is to manufacture indebtedness the recipient did not choose.

sources: Gouldner (1960), American Sociological Review 25:161–178
Regan (1971), Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 7:627–639
Burger, Horita, Kinoshita, Roberts & Vera (1997) — replication
Whatley, Webster, Smith & Rhodes (1999), Basic and Applied Social Psychology 21:251–259 — public versus private compliance
Goldstein, Griskevicius & Cialdini (2011) — reciprocity by proxy
open: Whether the effect size has ever been meta-analysed directly. I found replications and boundary studies but no meta-analysis of reciprocity-induced compliance.

label: Commitment & consistency

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: Multiple meta-analyses exist and they identify the specific experimental conditions most likely to produce the effect, which is a different kind of claim from 'this works'. Sequential-request techniques are also not interchangeable: one comparison found door-in-the-face produced 75.8% compliance against foot-in-the-door's 48.5% on the same target request.
strength.magnitude: The oldest and most researched of the sequential-request procedures, examined in more than a hundred published studies with several reviews and meta-analyses behind it.
strength.boundaries: The finding that forces a downgrade: the same review concludes the technique can be ineffective, and in some conditions can lead to a decrease in compliance. It is not a lever that reliably points one way. Effects are also moderated by disposition — several studies found the foot-in-the-door effect for participants high in preference for consistency but not for those low on it.

body.def: Once people commit — especially publicly, actively and effortfully — they behave consistently with it. The applied form is foot-in-the-door: a small request first, a larger related one later.
body.mech: Re-audited in Cycle 8, and the mechanism turns out to be plural rather than singular. A major review identifies at least six processes that a foot-in-the-door manipulation can set in motion: self-perception, psychological reactance, conformity, consistency, attributions, and commitment — and argues their combined effects account for both successful demonstrations and the studies where the technique was ineffective.
body.app: Downgraded from solid to moderate. The principle is real and conditional. Banking a small yes helps with people already disposed toward consistency, in the right conditions, and can backfire outside them.

sources: Freedman & Fraser (1966), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Burger (1999), Personality and Social Psychology Review 3(4):303–325 — multiple-process analysis and review
Beaman, Cole, Preston, Klentz & Steblay (1983), PSPB — fifteen years of foot-in-the-door research
Dillard, Hunter & Burgoon (1984), Human Communication Research 10:461–488
Cialdini, Vincent, Lewis, Catalan, Wheeler & Darby (1975) — door-in-the-face
open: Whether the technique has a net positive effect averaged across realistic conditions, given that some conditions reduce compliance.

label: Social proof

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: A separate US study with almost 400 observations per condition found a purely descriptive general norm failed to increase reuse compared to control; only combining descriptive with injunctive norms changed behaviour. A direct replication in Austria and Switzerland found a same-room advantage over general norms but no overall advantage of either over the standard appeal. The replication authors note baseline reuse was dramatically higher in Europe (70–90%) than the US (35–50%), and argue that identical wording can carry different meaning across cultures — a real defence, and also an admission that the effect is context-dependent in ways the principle as popularly stated is not.
strength.magnitude: Re-audited in Cycle 4 against its most cited applied demonstration — the hotel towel study — and the result is not what the principle's popularity implies. The original found descriptive norm messages outperformed a standard environmental appeal (44.1% vs 35.1% reuse), and that a 'provincial' norm referring to guests in the same room beat other norms (49.3% vs 42.8%) and the standard message (37.2%).
strength.boundaries: Direct replication in two German hotels found the opposite in places. In Study 1 (N=724) the four descriptive-norm conditions combined (81.9%) did not beat the standard environmental message (83.7%), and the same-room provincial norm produced a significantly lower compliance rate (78.0%) than the general hotel-guest norm (85.6%) — a reversal of the original. In Study 2 (N=204) any message beat no message (79.6% vs 64.3%), but the standard environmental message (93.3%) was more effective than the descriptive norms combined (76.5%).

body.def: The principle that under uncertainty people copy what similar others do, and that telling people most others already do something increases compliance.
body.mech: Descriptive norms tell people what behaviour is likely to be appropriate and effective in a situation. Injunctive norms tell them what is approved. The two are distinguishable and appear to behave differently.
body.app: Social proof is sold as a reliable lever. The evidence supports something narrower: norm messages can work, they often need an injunctive component, the provincial-norm refinement does not reliably replicate and has reversed, and in a population already disposed toward the behaviour a straightforward content appeal can outperform the norm message entirely. Downgraded from solid to contested on this basis.

sources: Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius (2008), Journal of Consumer Research 35:472–482 — the original
Bohner & Schlüter (2014), PLOS ONE 9(8):e104086 — direct and extended replication, N=724 and N=204
Schultz, Khazian & Zaleski (2008), Social Influence 3:4–23
Reese, Loew & Steffgen (2014), Journal of Social Psychology 154:97–100
Nolan, Schultz, Cialdini, Goldstein & Griskevicius (2008), PSPB — normative influence is underdetected
open: Whether descriptive norms work at all without an injunctive component, and whether the technique has any reliable effect in populations already inclined toward the behaviour.

label: Authority

body.def: Credible expertise and status signals increase compliance, often automatically.
body.mech: Titles, uniforms and accurate specifics. Milgram's obedience work is the famous and interpretively contested demonstration.
body.app: One accurate technical detail early outperforms a credentials list.

sources: Cialdini (2021), Influence

label: Obedience (Milgram)

body.def: A majority of participants delivered what they believed were dangerous shocks under instruction.
body.mech: Legitimate authority plus incremental escalation. Archival work shows compliance varied with how the prods were framed and that many participants doubted the setup.
body.app: Incremental escalation inside a legitimate frame moves people further than any single request.

sources: Milgram (1963), Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
Burger (2009), American Psychologist — partial replication
Perry (2013), Behind the Shock Machine — archival critique

label: Liking

body.def: We agree more readily with people we like — driven by attractiveness, similarity, compliments, cooperation and familiarity.
body.mech: Largely warmth-axis perception with halo spillover.
body.app: Cooperative framing outperforms charm. Note the ceiling: being liked is not sufficient in complex decisions.

sources: Cialdini (2021), Influence
Byrne (1971), The Attraction Paradigm

label: Scarcity & reactance

strength.label: moderate
strength.replication: The effect is real but conditional on type, expectation and perceived sincerity — a materially weaker claim than the principle as it is sold. Downgraded from solid to moderate.
strength.magnitude: Re-audited in Cycle 8. Meta-analytic work supports the effect for demand-based and time-based scarcity. Supply-based scarcity is where it gets complicated.
strength.boundaries: Scarcity can reverse. Four experiments and a field study found that limited quantities lower than consumers expected undermine perceived retailer sincerity and, through that, reduce purchase likelihood. Earlier work also found quantity scarcity raises only the subjective value of a good and not its assessed market value — so the mechanism may not be the 'it must be expensive' inference usually assumed. Evidence on that inference is described in the literature as mixed.

body.def: Perceived scarcity or threatened access raises perceived value and urgency. In marketing it appears as limited quantity, limited time, restricted access, high demand or claimed uniqueness.
body.mech: Commodity theory plus reactance — the push-back triggered when freedom of choice is threatened. A meta-analysis categorises the effect into demand-based, supply-based and time-based scarcity, which behave differently.
body.app: Genuine constraints are legitimate and effective. Manufactured urgency carries a documented failure mode: when the stated limit reads as implausible, it damages trust in the source and reduces the very behaviour it was meant to increase. That is the empirical version of the warning that manipulative scarcity costs you the warmth axis.

sources: Worchel, Lee & Adewole (1975), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Brehm (1966), A Theory of Psychological Reactance
Barton, Zlatevska & Oppewal (2022), Journal of Retailing — meta-analysis of product scarcity on purchase intentions
Ladeira, Lim, de Oliveira Santini, Rasul, Perin & Altinay (2023), Psychology & Marketing 40 — meta-analysis on product scarcity
When product scarcity backfires (2025), Journal of Retailing — five studies on limited quantities and perceived sincerity
Lynn (1992); Abendroth & Diehl (2006) — subjective versus market value
open: Whether scarcity has any net positive effect once the sincerity backfire is priced in across realistic commercial conditions.

label: Conformity (Asch)

body.def: People conform to a unanimous majority even against clear perceptual evidence, and conformity drops sharply with a single dissenter.
body.mech: Normative influence (fitting in) and informational influence (assuming others know).
body.app: One visible ally breaks a consensus in a group decision.

sources: Bond & Smith (1996), Psychological Bulletin — meta-analysis
open: Bond & Smith found the effect varies by culture and has declined over time. Magnitude not re-verified this cycle.

label: Social identity theory

body.def: Part of self-concept derives from group membership, and even arbitrary group assignment produces in-group favouritism.
body.mech: Minimal-group paradigm; self-esteem partly derives from in-group standing.
body.app: Shared identity builds 'us' faster than shared time does.

sources: Tajfel & Turner (1979)
Tajfel, Billig, Bundy & Flament (1971), European Journal of Social Psychology

label: Self-efficacy

body.def: Belief in your capability to execute a specific task predicts effort, persistence and performance. Built by mastery experience, vicarious experience, persuasion and physiological state, in descending order of strength.
body.mech: Task-specific rather than global confidence.
body.app: Small real wins build it. Give someone a mastery experience before asking for a large commitment.

sources: Bandura (1977), Psychological Review
Bandura (1997), Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control

label: Emotion regulation

body.def: Five points at which an emotion can be regulated: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive reappraisal, response modulation. Reappraisal generally outperforms suppression.
body.mech: Earlier interventions are cheaper; suppression costs memory and rapport.
body.app: Change the situation or the interpretation before trying to change the feeling.

sources: Gross (1998), Review of General Psychology
Gross (2015), Psychological Inquiry

label: Growth mindset

plain.what: Believing your ability can improve rather than being fixed.
plain.why: It was sold as a general performance lever for schools and workplaces; the measured averages are far smaller than the promise.
plain.catch: It helps mainly where a fixed belief was actively stopping someone from trying. It is not a boost for people who were already trying.

body.def: The belief that ability is malleable. Claimed effects are large; meta-analytic averages are small and concentrated in at-risk students.
body.mech: Appears to work where the belief was actively blocking effort, not as a general performance lever.
body.app: Useful as a stance, weak as an intervention. Do not build a training program on it.

sources: Dweck (2006), Mindset
Sisk, Burgoyne, Sun, Butler & Macnamara (2018), Psychological Science — meta-analyses
Yeager et al. (2019), Nature

label: Ego depletion

plain.what: The idea that willpower runs out like a fuel tank.
plain.why: It shaped a decade of self-control advice before large multi-lab re-tests came back flat.
plain.catch: People who believe willpower runs out behave as though it does. The belief may be doing the work the biology was credited with.

body.def: The claim that willpower is a limited resource depleted by use.
body.mech: Original effects appear to have been driven by publication bias and by participants' beliefs about willpower.
body.app: Do not build routines on conserving willpower. Build them on environment design.

sources: Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven & Tice (1998), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Hagger et al. (2016), Perspectives on Psychological Science — multi-site replication
Vohs et al. (2021), Psychological Science

label: Power posing

plain.what: Standing in a big confident pose was supposed to change your hormones. It does not.
plain.why: It was one of the most-watched ideas in the history of psychology, and the hormone claim did not survive re-testing.
plain.catch: Two things did survive: you may feel more powerful, and other people do read your posture. Nothing measurable happens in your blood.

body.def: Expansive posture was claimed to raise testosterone, lower cortisol and increase risk-taking. The hormonal and behavioural claims failed replication; self-reported felt power survived.
body.mech: Posture is still read by others, which is a perception effect rather than a physiological one.
body.app: Open posture for the audience, not for your endocrine system.

sources: Carney, Cuddy & Yap (2010), Psychological Science
Ranehill et al. (2015), Psychological Science — replication failure
Simmons & Simonsohn (2017), Psychological Science

label: Delay of gratification

body.def: Delay of gratification in early childhood was reported to predict later life outcomes. A larger replication found a much smaller association, largely explained by family background.
body.mech: v1 attributed the shrinkage to 'trust in the reliability of the environment'. That was one hypothesis stated as the explanation. The replication's own finding was that family background accounts for most of it — and Cycle 1 supplies a better-specified version of what family background contains: passive gene–environment correlation, in which parents supply both genotype and environment, plus genetic nurture. The trust account may also be true; it is not what the replication showed.
body.app: Self-control is real as a trait; the single-test destiny story is not.

sources: Mischel, Shoda & Rodriguez (1989), Science
Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018), Psychological Science — replication
open: How much of the residual association is genetic confounding versus environmental. Not resolved, and v1 implied it was.

label: Oxytocin as 'trust hormone'

body.def: Intranasal oxytocin was reported to increase trust in a widely cited 2005 study. It has not replicated reliably.
body.mech: Small samples and publication bias produced an effect that larger analyses do not support.
body.app: Any technique sold as triggering oxytocin is selling a story.

sources: Kosfeld, Heinrichs, Zak, Fischbacher & Fehr (2005), Nature
Nave, Camerer & McCullough (2015), Perspectives on Psychological Science

label: Adult attachment

strength.label: solid
strength.replication: The dimensional structure replicates well. The continuity claim does not fare as well, and Cycle 6 re-audited it with figures. Fraley's meta-analysis found security moderately stable across the first 19 years, best described by prototype rather than revisionist dynamics. A meta-analysis restricted to strange-situation-based methods found only moderate stability across early childhood — κ = 0.23 for four-way classification, r = 0.28 secure/insecure. In a 20-year longitudinal study, 72% kept the same secure/insecure classification from infancy to early adulthood (κ = .44) — but 44% of those whose mothers reported negative life events changed classification, against 22% of those without. For adult self-report measures, typical stability coefficients run .50 to .60 over spans from two weeks to two decades. Moderate is the right word throughout, and the popular version is not moderate.
strength.magnitude: The original study analysed 620 responses to a 'love quiz' printed in a newspaper, reporting roughly 56% secure, 25% avoidant and 19% anxious — a distribution the authors noted resembled infant findings. The two-dimensional structure was subsequently confirmed by confirmatory factor analysis, which found a two-dimensional model fit better than three- or one-dimensional alternatives.
strength.boundaries: The founding sample was self-selected newspaper respondents, skewed female (415 of 620), and relied on retrospective recall of childhood — three limitations v1 omitted entirely. Cycle 1 adds a fourth: parent–child concordance in attachment cannot be read as pure environmental transmission, because genetic nurture research shows parent-to-child similarity in socially mediated outcomes is substantially confounded with shared genotype.

plain.what: How you behave in close relationships, described by two dials: how much you fear being left, and how uncomfortable closeness makes you.
plain.why: It is the most useful thing here for understanding why people cling, pull away, or do both.
plain.catch: Not three fixed types, despite how it is always presented. And the settings move with later experience.

body.def: Infant attachment theory extended to adult romantic bonds. Best represented not as three types but as two continuous dimensions: attachment anxiety (fear of abandonment, hypervigilance to a partner's availability) and avoidance (discomfort with closeness and dependence).
body.mech: Internal working models of self and other, formed in early relationships and revisable through later experience.
body.intra: Your reaction to a partner's silence is diagnostic of where you sit on the anxiety dimension.
body.inter: Intermittent, unpredictable availability selectively engages people high in attachment anxiety and repels secure ones. A tactic 'working' may mean it selected for anxiety rather than that it built attraction.
body.app: The same architecture governs client dependence: reliability builds a secure base, unpredictability produces either anxious over-checking or withdrawal.

sources: Hazan & Shaver (1987), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — N=620
Brennan, Clark & Shaver (1998) — Experiences in Close Relationships
Sharpley & Rogers (1997), Journal of Social and Personal Relationships — two-dimensional CFA, N=571
Fraley (2002), Personality and Social Psychology Review 6(2) — meta-analysis and dynamic modelling of stability from infancy to adulthood
Waters, Merrick, Treboux, Crowell & Albersheim (2000), Child Development — 20-year longitudinal, 72% same classification
Opie et al. — early childhood attachment stability meta-analysis, κ=0.23 / r=0.28
Fraley & Brumbaugh (2004) — adult stability coefficients .50–.60
open: Cycle 6 partially answered this. Within-person work using interrupted time-series found about a quarter of life events related to enduring attachment change, with average enduring effects under 0.10 SD but very large individual differences — the likelihood of shifting by more than a third of a standard deviation ranged from 5% to 86% depending on the event. People also tended to become less anxious over time regardless of events. What remains open is why the individual differences are that large.

label: Triangular theory of love

body.def: Love as three components — intimacy, passion, commitment — whose combinations produce different relationship types. A measurement model more than a causal theory.
body.mech: Passion rises and falls fastest; intimacy and commitment carry the long term.
body.app: Seduction frameworks are almost entirely a passion toolkit and say little about the other two.

sources: Sternberg (1986), Psychological Review

label: Investment model of commitment

body.def: Commitment is predicted by satisfaction plus investment size minus quality of alternatives.
body.mech: All three terms contribute independently, so people leave when alternatives improve, not only when satisfaction drops.
body.app: Retention requires raising satisfaction, deepening investment, and being better than the alternative — all three.

sources: Rusbult (1980), Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
Le & Agnew (2003), Personal Relationships — meta-analysis

label: Conflict patterns in couples

strength.label: contested
strength.replication: The Gottman Institute's own FAQ acknowledges the confusion over the accuracy figures and reframes the claim as identifying that a couple is behaving like couples in the group that later divorced — which is a materially weaker statement than predicting divorce. Gottman and Levenson's own 2002 discussion describes their analyses as post hoc and their conclusions as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
strength.magnitude: Re-audited in Cycle 3 with the actual numbers. Heyman and Smith Slep demonstrated the problem rather than arguing it: they took 528 people from the 1985 National Family Violence Survey — 176 divorced, 352 married or cohabiting — split them randomly into halves of 264, built a divorce-prediction equation on the first half in the standard way, and tested it on the second. On the half it was built from, overall accuracy was 90%, sensitivity 92%, specificity 89%, and when it predicted divorce it was right 65% of the time. On fresh data, sensitivity fell by 45% and specificity by 15%.
strength.boundaries: An independent generalizability test applied the affective process models to 85 married or cohabiting couples from an at-risk community sample assessed around age 21 and followed up two and a half years later. Several specific mechanisms did not predict relationship status: men's rejection of their partner's influence, men's failure to de-escalate a partner's negative affect, and women's negative start-up.

body.def: Observed interaction patterns — criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling — and a positive-to-negative ratio during conflict, claimed to distinguish stable from distressed couples and to predict divorce with very high accuracy.
body.mech: The behavioural patterns themselves are observable and the descriptive work is real. The prediction claims are where the problem sits.
body.inter: The descriptive content is the useful part and it does not depend on the prediction claims. Contempt as the strongest negative marker, and repair attempts mattering more than avoiding conflict, are worth keeping.
body.app: The 90%-plus divorce prediction figure is quoted constantly in popular relationship writing and in business books about communication. It is an in-sample fit statistic. A model that hits 90% on its training data can drop to a 29% positive predictive value on fresh data, which is what Heyman and Slep demonstrated with their own equation.

sources: Gottman & Levenson (1992), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Heyman & Smith Slep (2001), Journal of Marriage and Family 63(2):473–479 — the hazards of predicting divorce without crossvalidation
Kim, Capaldi & Crosby (2007), Journal of Marriage and Family — generalizability test, N=85 at-risk couples
Gottman & Levenson (2002) — authors' own description of the analyses as post hoc
open: Whether any of the specific mechanisms predict out of sample in a general population. The one independent test found several did not.

label: Mate preferences across cultures

body.def: Kindness, intelligence and health rank at or near the top for both sexes across large cross-cultural samples, with moderate and replicable sex differences in the relative emphasis on resources versus physical attractiveness.
body.mech: Evolved preferences calibrated by local conditions.
body.app: The top-ranked traits are the two social-evaluation dimensions in another vocabulary.

sources: Buss (1989), Behavioral and Brain Sciences
Walter et al. (2020), Psychological Science — multi-country replication
open: Whether sex differences shrink with gender equality is disputed and was not verified this cycle.

label: SPIN Selling
